question: What were the main findings of the A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes.txt clinical trial?
passage_1: "A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes (TODAY)” study evaluates the efficacy of three treatment regimens—metformin alone, metformin combined with rosiglitazone, and metformin combined with an intensive lifestyle-intervention program—in achieving durable glycemic control among children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that metformin plus rosiglitazone was particularly effective in girls, while metformin monotherapy was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants. Serious adverse events occurred in 19.2% of participants across the trial, and although the paper does not explicitly state formal clinical recommendations or guidelines, it concludes that metformin monotherapy fails to maintain durable glycemic control in roughly half of youth with type 2 diabetes and that adding rosiglitazone provides superior glycemic durability compared to monotherapy or intensive lifestyle interventions.
passage_2: "Treatment with canagliflozin versus placebo in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes: a randomized clinical trial" reported that treatment options for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are limited. Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of T2DM in adults. The objective was to assess the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin in children and adolescents with T2DM. This was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03170518; EudraCT: 2016-005223-88) conducted at 104 sites in 10 countries. Participants were children and adolescents aged 10 years or older with T2DM (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] ≥6.5% to ≤11%). Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The treatment period was 52 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, along with secondary efficacy end points and safety. A total of 171 participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (n = 84) or placebo (n = 87). At week 26, HbA1c reduction from baseline was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (difference in least-squares means, -0.76% [95% CI, -1.25% to -0.27%]; P = 0.002). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). Treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) occurred in 77.4% and 74.7% and serious treatment-emergent AEs in 9.5% and 5.7% of participants who received canagliflozin and placebo, respectively.
passage_3: "Efficacy and safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin versus placebo and the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin versus placebo in youth with type 2 diabetes: a multicentre, randomised, doubleblind, parallel group, phase 3 trial" evaluates the efficacy and safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin (10 mg or 25 mg daily) and the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin (5 mg daily) compared to a shared placebo over 26 weeks in youth aged 10–17 years with type 2 diabetes who were previously treated with metformin and/or insulin. The study found that empagliflozin provided a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in HbA1c baseline levels compared to placebo (-0.84%, p=0.012), whereas linagliptin did not show a statistically significant reduction (-0.34%, p=0.29). Hypoglycemia was the most frequently reported adverse event, with higher rates observed in active treatment groups, though no severe hypoglycemia cases occurred. Based on these findings, the paper suggests that empagliflozin may offer a valuable new oral treatment option for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes to address the therapeutic unmet need in this population.

question: What methodology was used in the A Multidisciplinary Approach to the Adolescent Bariatric Surgical Patient.txt study?
passage_1: "A Multidisciplinary Approach to the Adolescent Bariatric Surgical Patient" evaluates the establishment, early outcomes, and multidisciplinary framework of a pediatric bariatric surgery program—specifically the Comprehensive Weight Management Center at Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center—for treating clinically severe obesity in adolescents. Examining referrals and initial surgical cases using Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGBP), the study found that RYGBP leads to significant, clinically meaningful weight loss and the reversal of severe comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea, though medical and behavioral complications can occur. The paper recommends managing adolescent bariatric surgery within a comprehensive, multidisciplinary team of pediatric specialists to address the unique medical, developmental, and psychosocial needs of young patients. Furthermore, it outlines clinical guidelines requiring candidates to have achieved most of their linear growth, have a BMI ≥40 with severe comorbidities or a BMI ≥50 with less severe comorbidities, and demonstrate the ability to commit to lifelong medical surveillance and dietary supplementation.
passage_2: "Teen-Longitudinal Assessment of Bariatric Surgery (Teen-LABS): Methodologic Features of the First Prospective Multicenter Study of Adolescent Bariatric Surgery" evaluates the methodological design and protocol of the first prospective, multicenter observational study designed to collect coordinated clinical, epidemiological, and behavioral data on adolescents (≤19 years old) undergoing bariatric surgery compared to adult historical counterparts. The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.
passage_3: "One-year outcomes of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbidly obese adolescents: a multicenter study from the Pediatric Bariatric Study Group" evaluates the 1-year weight loss, metabolic changes, and complications following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGBP) in a multicenter cohort of 36 morbidly obese adolescents (ages 13–21) compared to a nonsurgical control group. The study found that surgical patients experienced a significant 37% drop in mean body mass index (from 56.5 kg/m² to 35.8 kg/m², alongside significant improvements in metabolic variables including triglycerides, total cholesterol, fasting blood glucose, and fasting insulin, whereas the nonsurgical group showed no statistically significant BMI change. While 61% of surgical patients had no complications, 15 patients experienced adverse events, including 9 minor complications, 4 moderate complications, and 2 severe medical complications (including one case of severe beriberi and one late death secondary to C. difficile colitis and multiorgan failure), with no perioperative deaths or severe surgical complications observed. The authors recommend close, multidisciplinary monitoring of adolescent bariatric patients to ensure nutritional compliance, detect complications early, and incorporate targeted interventions like B-complex vitamin supplementation, while highlighting the need for further prospective studies to better define indications, surgical options, and long-term safety guidelines.

question: What population was studied in the A Nonlinear Effect of Hyperglycemia and Current Cigarette Smoking Are Major Determinants of the Onset of Microalbuminuria in Type 1 Diabetes.txt study?
passage_1: "A Nonlinear Effect of Hyperglycemia and Current Cigarette Smoking Are Major Determinants of the Onset of Microalbuminuria in Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the temporal and joint effects of glycemic control (measured by HbA1c) and cigarette smoking status on the 4-year incidence of microalbuminuria among 943 young adults with type 1 diabetes from the Natural History of Microalbuminuria Study. The findings demonstrate that microalbuminuria developed at a rate of 3.3 per 100 person-years, with recent HbA1c levels (from the 1st and 2nd years preceding onset) serving as a stronger predictor of risk than older or cumulative 4-year measurements, indicating an attenuation of the impact of past hyperglycemia over time. The study identified a significant nonlinear relationship between HbA1c and microalbuminuria risk, showing a markedly steeper increase in risk once HbA1c exceeds 8%, a risk enhancement that is further magnified among current cigarette smokers (who experienced an incidence rate of 7.9 per 100 person-years compared to 1.8 for past smokers and 2.2 for never-smokers). While no explicit clinical guidelines or recommendations are formally established in the text, the authors conclude that patients with type 1 diabetes who smoke and maintain HbA1c levels above 8% face the highest risk for developing microalbuminuria.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.
passage_3: "Prevalence of Tobacco Use and Association between Cardiometabolic Risk Factors and Cigarette Smoking in Youth with Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus" evaluates the prevalence of tobacco use and its association with cardiometabolic risk factors among youth aged 10 to 22 years with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus using data from the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study. The findings demonstrate that tobacco use is prevalent in this population, increasing significantly with age and reaching 34.0% in youth ≥20 years with type 1 diabetes and 40.3% in those with type 2 diabetes, with higher smoking rates among youth from lower-income families (<$50,000). Furthermore, current cigarette smoking in youth with type 1 diabetes was significantly associated with higher odds of high triglyceride levels and physical inactivity, alongside less favorable overall cardiometabolic risk profiles across both diabetes types. Despite these risks, less than half of younger participants (aged 10–14 years) reported ever receiving counseling from a healthcare provider to avoid or quit smoking. Based on these observations, the paper recommends that aggressive tobacco prevention and smoking cessation programs be made a high priority in clinical care to prevent or delay the onset of cardiovascular disease in youth with diabetes mellitus.

passage_1: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.

In the current study, we examined whether CD affects the risk of diabetic retinopathy (DRP) in patients with T1D. This was a population-based cohort study. Through the Swedish National Patient Register, we identified 41,566 patients diagnosed with diabetes in 1964–2009 and who were ≤30 years of age at diagnosis. CD was defined as having villous atrophy (Marsh stage 3) according to small intestinal biopsies performed between 1969 and 2008, with biopsy reports obtained from Sweden’s 28 pathology departments. During follow-up, 947 T1D patients had a diagnosis of CD. We used Cox regression analysis with CD as a time-dependent covariate to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for DRP in patients with T1D and CD and compared them with patients with T1D but no CD. Duration of CD correlated with the risk of DRP. When results were stratified by time since CD diagnosis, individuals with T1D and CD were at a lower risk of DRP in the first 5 years after CD diagnosis (aHR 0.57 [95% CI 0.36–0.91]), followed by a neutral risk in years 5 to <10 (1.03 [0.68–1.57]). With longer follow-up, coexisting CD was a risk factor for DRP (10 to <15 years of follow-up, aHR 2.83 [95% CI 1.95–4.11]; ≥15 years of follow-up, 3.01 [1.43–6.32]). We concluded that having a diagnosis of CD for >10 years is a risk factor for the development of DRP in T1D. Long-standing CD in patients with T1D merits intense monitoring of DRP.

The findings reveal that CGM sensors generally overestimate capillary blood glucose levels, particularly during low-intensity continuous exercise and low- or high-intensity interval exercise, but demonstrate clinically acceptable overall performance across most conditions except during high-intensity continuous exercise. Based on these results, the paper recommends using CGM to help avoid exercise-induced hypoglycemia during physical activity, but provides the guideline that standard capillary blood glucose monitoring should still be performed alongside CGM during high-intensity exercise to ensure safety and prevent unmanaged glycemic events.

The findings indicate that physical exercise negatively impacts sensor accuracy, causing sensors to consistently overestimate blood glucose levels—a performance drop that was significantly more pronounced during moderate continuous exercise than during interval exercise. question: What population was studied in the Adaptation of an Adult Web Application for Type 1 Diabetes Self-management to Youth Using the Behavior Change Wheel to Tailor the Needs of Health Care Transition Qualitative Interview Study.txt study?
passage_1: "Adaptation of an Adult Web Application for Type 1 Diabetes Self-management to Youth Using the Behavior Change Wheel to Tailor the Needs of Health Care Transition: Qualitative Interview Study" evaluates the needs and factors influencing diabetes self-management among youth aged 14 to 24 living with type 1 diabetes to guide the adaptation of an adult self-guided web application (Support). The findings categorize self-management factors into internal and external barriers and facilitators, highlighting that youth desire reliable, practical, and novel educational content, alongside supervised peer exchange and simplified information search processes, to navigate the challenges of transitioning to adult care.
passage_2: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

The findings indicate that out of 182 participants, 56% transferred to adult care, 15% received no care, and 29% remained in pediatric care, with higher age at diagnosis and longer diabetes duration predicting the departure from pediatric care. Furthermore, transferring to adult care or receiving no care was significantly associated with higher odds of poor glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥ 9.0%), independent of sex, race, ethnicity, or baseline HbA1c levels. Recommendations and guidelines provided in the paper emphasize the urgent need for tailored clinical programs, healthcare system policies, targeted treatments, patient-centered care, and early education for both adult specialists and generalists to support the growing population of young adults with youth-onset Type 2 diabetes and prevent disease deterioration during the transition period.

passage_1: The study Alterations in White Matter Structure in Young Children With Type 1 Diabetes evaluates whether type 1 diabetes affects white matter brain structure in young children (ages 4 to <10 years) by utilizing diffusion tensor imaging to analyze axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and fractional anisotropy in relation to continuous glucose monitoring metrics, glycemic history, and cognitive function. Results demonstrate that young children with type 1 diabetes exhibit widespread reductions in axial diffusivity across multiple brain regions compared to healthy controls, with microstructural changes significantly driven by chronic hyperglycemia—including elevated HbA1c levels and prolonged glucose elevations above 180, 250, and 300 mg/dL—as well as high glucose variability. Higher blood glucose metrics and erratic fluctuations correspond with decreased fractional anisotropy and increased radial diffusivity, pointing to altered myelination and axonal integrity, whereas hypoglycemic events and severe hypoglycemic seizures show no significant association with white matter structural alterations. Furthermore, fractional anisotropy levels directly correlate with Full-Scale IQ in pediatric diabetes patients, confirming the functional relevance of these white matter changes during early neurodevelopment. While the findings do not establish direct clinical practice guidelines, the clear clinical recommendation for treating pediatric type 1 diabetes is to reorient management strategies toward minimizing chronic hyperglycemia and smoothing out sharp glucose fluctuations rather than focusing predominantly on avoiding hypoglycemia, utilizing continuous glucose monitoring to actively suppress high blood sugar spikes and safeguard early brain development and cognitive potential.
passage_2: The study Neurological Consequences of Diabetic Ketoacidosis at Initial Presentation of Type 1 Diabetes in a Prospective Cohort Study of Children evaluates the acute and medium-term impacts of new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) on brain morphology and cognitive function in children newly diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes. By assessing children aged 6 to 18 years at baseline, day 5, day 28, and 6 months using MRI, MRS, and cognitive testing, the study highlights how DKA alters cerebral structure and neurocognitive performance even without the presence of severe clinical cerebral edema. The findings reveal that children presenting with DKA experience significant changes in white and gray matter structures, including higher total white matter volume and increased mean diffusivity in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes at presentation, alongside reduced total cortical gray matter volume and lower levels of N-acetylaspartate in the frontal gray matter and basal ganglia. Although acute structural and volume changes resolved over time, DKA presentation was associated with persistent adverse functional outcomes at the 6-month follow-up, specifically lower delayed memory recall, poorer sustained and divided attention, and reduced baseline mental state scores. Furthermore, lower blood pH at presentation and younger age were identified as key predictors of both structural brain changes and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. The recommendations and guidelines stemming from this study emphasize the critical need to view DKA-related brain injury along a continuous spectrum rather than as an isolated risk limited to overt cerebral edema. Clinicians and healthcare providers are urged to prioritize early detection and prompt intervention for Type 1 Diabetes in pediatric patients to prevent initial DKA episodes entirely, thereby protecting vulnerable developing brain tissue.

Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

question: What were the main findings of the American College of Gastroenterology Guidelines Update Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease.txt study?
passage_1: "American College of Gastroenterology guidelines update: diagnosis and management of celiac disease" guideline presents an update to the 2013 American College of Gastroenterology Guideline on the Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease with updated recommendations for the evaluation and management of patients with celiac disease (CD). CD is defined as a permanent immune-mediated response to gluten present in wheat, barley, and rye. CD has a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations that resemble a multisystemic disorder rather than an isolated intestinal disease, and is characterized by small bowel injury and the presence of specific antibodies. Detection of CD-specific antibodies (e.g., tissue transglutaminase) in the serum is very helpful for the initial screening of patients with suspicion of CD. Intestinal biopsy is required in most patients to confirm the diagnosis. A nonbiopsy strategy for the diagnosis of CD in selected children is suggested and discussed in detail. Current treatment for CD requires strict adherence to a gluten-free diet (GFD) and lifelong medical follow-up. Most patients have excellent clinical response to a GFD. Nonresponsive CD is defined by persistent or recurrent symptoms despite being on a GFD. These patients require a systematic workup to rule out specific conditions that may cause persistent or recurrent symptoms, especially unintentional gluten contamination. Refractory CD is a rare cause of nonresponsive CD often associated with poor prognosis.
passage_2: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.
passage_3: This perspective article from Diabetes Care, titled Adult-Onset Type 1 Diabetes: Current Understanding and Challenges, summarizes the outcomes of an international JDRF expert workshop aimed at improving the clinical understanding, diagnostic accuracy, and management of adult-onset type 1 diabetes. The primary objective of the workshop and paper is to address the widespread issue of misdiagnosis, as over half of all new type 1 diabetes cases occur in adults, yet nearly 40% are initially misclassified—most commonly as type 2 diabetes due to slower metabolic progression and overlapping clinical traits. By highlighting the distinct epidemiological, immunogenetic, and metabolic features of adult-onset cases, the authors seek to establish clearer diagnostic frameworks and treatment guidelines for practicing clinicians. To evaluate potential cases effectively, the authors provide the diagnostic "AABBCC" framework, guiding clinicians to systematically assess Age at onset, Autoimmunity via islet autoantibody testing, Body habitus and BMI, family and personal background, glycemic Control trajectory, and associated Comorbidities such as thyroid autoimmunity or celiac disease. For laboratory guidelines, the authors recommend ordering islet autoantibody assays as the primary test for short-duration disease (under three years), with serum glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies serving as the predominant marker. For disease durations exceeding three years, C-peptide testing paired with blood glucose is recommended as the main tool to measure remaining beta-cell function. Regarding therapeutic management, the paper outlines guidelines based on C-peptide levels and disease characteristics. Patients with random C-peptide levels at or below 300 pmol/L require primary insulin therapy.

Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.

Analyzing a cohort of 7,549 participants, the study found an overall MA prevalence of 4.4% (329 participants), with a higher frequency strongly associated with longer diabetes duration, higher mean glycosylated hemoglobin HbA1c, older age, female sex, higher diastolic blood pressure, and lower BMI z score, while MA was uncommon (<2%) in individuals with an average HbA1c <7.5%. Despite MA diagnosis, only 36% of affected participants were currently receiving ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker treatment. Based on these findings, the authors emphasize the critical need for optimal glycemic and blood pressure control to reduce nephropathy risk, and they highlight ADA screening guidelines recommending annual MA screening in individuals with type 1 diabetes starting at 10 years of age and 5 years of diabetes duration to ensure early diagnosis and timely intervention.

This review paper aims to provide a comprehensive examination of pediatric psychologists’ roles in working with children and adolescents with diabetes, including during distinct phases of treatment (e.g., diagnosis, outpatient diabetes clinic visits, inpatient hospitalizations, and outpatient psychology visits) and with different modalities of psychological interventions (e.g., screening, individual, family, and group therapy). In addition, the role of the psychologist in diabetes care within various settings (e.g., private practice, academic medical centers, and community organizations) will be explored. Finally, this paper will outline other roles in which psychologists contribute to diabetes-specific efforts (e.g., translational research, program development in transition to adult care, advocacy for health care reform initiatives, health care billing/reimbursement, and alternative methods to psychosocial care delivery) as well as future directions for working with children and adolescents with diabetes. Pediatric psychologists have multiple professional roles in a wide variety of settings; however, there is more that can be done in the future to fully utilize pediatric psychologists in diabetes care for children and adolescents, such as embedding psychologists into integrated clinic visits where families receive comprehensive medical and psychological services to support overall health and well-being. Therefore, there is a need for increased advocacy to obtain even more pediatric psychology engagement in diabetes care to provide new clinical services and develop more translational research.

question: What were the main findings of the An Evaluation of Recurrent Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Fragmentation of Care, and Mortality Across Chicago, Illinois.txt study?
passage_1: "An Evaluation of Recurrent Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Fragmentation of Care, and Mortality Across Chicago, Illinois" evaluates recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), healthcare fragmentation, and all-cause mortality using a deidentified EHR dataset from six Chicago-area institutions covering 3,615 patients with DKA between 2006 and 2012. The study found that 21.6% of patients experienced recurrent DKA, with those having four or more episodes accounting for 26.3% of total encounters, and 16% of recurrent patients experienced fragmented care across multiple hospitals, which was significantly associated with higher recurrence rates and increased mean HbA1c levels. Furthermore, 13.6% of patients died during the study period, with mortality significantly associated with increasing age and a higher number of DKA encounters, though care fragmentation itself was not an independent factor in mortality. The authors conclude that recurrent DKA is a common, high-risk, and potentially avoidable challenge heavily linked to healthcare fragmentation and mortality, and they recommend that future public health efforts and research focus on early identification, tracking, and improved continuity of care for this unique patient population.
passage_2: The study Racial/Ethnic Minority Youth With Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Have Poor Prognostic Factors evaluates differences across racial and ethnic groups in characteristics known to influence long-term health outcomes at type 1 diabetes diagnosis and during the first three years post-diagnosis among youth under 19 years old. Analyzing 927 participants from the Pediatric Diabetes Consortium, the authors found that African American participants, compared to non-Hispanic Whites, presented with higher body mass index percentiles, more advanced pubertal development, and a higher frequency of diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis—a disparity largely explained by socioeconomic factors like health insurance—while also experiencing higher rates of hypertension, severe hypoglycemia, higher HbA1c levels, higher required insulin doses, and lower rates of entering partial remission over three years. Similarly, Hispanic participants exhibited higher BMI percentiles at diagnosis and throughout follow-up, a higher prevalence of dyslipidemia, and sustained trajectories of higher insulin doses and IDAA1c compared to non-Hispanic Whites. Based on these findings, the paper emphasizes that identifying markers that covary with race and ethnicity and predict clinical outcomes is critical before targeted interventions can be designed, highlighting the need to understand the basis of these racial disparities to design effective strategies that improve diabetes care and mitigate the elevated risk of long-term complications in minority youth
passage_3: The “Trends in the prevalence of ketoacidosis at diabetes diagnosis: the SEARCH for diabetes in youth study“ evaluates temporal changes in the prevalence of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at the time of diabetes diagnosis among youth aged 0 to 19 years, along with associated risk factors, across three time periods between 2002 and 2010. The study found that DKA prevalence at diagnosis among youth with type 1 diabetes remained persistently high and stable over time at approximately one-third of cases (30.2% in 2002–2003 to 31.1% in 2008–2010), with higher risk associated with younger age, ethnic minority status, lower household income, and lack of private health insurance. In contrast, DKA prevalence among youth with type 2 diabetes decreased significantly from 11.7% in 2002–2003 to 5.7% in 2008–2010 (an approximately 10% annual decline), with higher risk associated with younger age, male gender, and minority race/ethnicity. Based on these findings, the paper highlights a persistent need for increased awareness of diabetes signs and symptoms among the public and healthcare providers, alongside improved access to healthcare, to reduce DKA occurrence at onset in youth with type 1 diabetes.

question: What were the main findings of the Are children with type 1 diabetes safe at school Examining parent perceptions.txt study?
passage_1: Are children with type 1 diabetes safe at school? Examining parent perceptions evaluates parent perceptions regarding the safety of, and satisfaction with, the diabetes care their children with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus receive at school. The study compares parents in permissive states—where trained non-medical school personnel are permitted to provide diabetes care—with parents in non-permissive states, where only licensed healthcare professionals can provide such care. The findings indicate that parents in permissive states perceive their children to be just as safe during both the regular school day and extracurricular activities as parents in non-permissive states. Furthermore, parental satisfaction regarding overall diabetes care and specific responses to hypo- or hyperglycemia shows no statistically significant differences across state types. Although nearly all schools maintain a health clinic or nurse's office, non-permissive state schools have full-time registered nurses present more frequently than permissive state schools. During regular hours, care is primarily delivered by school nurses and the students themselves, while parents and students handle the majority of care during extracurricular activities, with over a third of parents reporting that they are required to attend outside-of-school events to manage their child's diabetes. Based on these findings, the study recommends that training non-medical school personnel is an effective strategy to maximize student safety and provide parental peace of mind when a full-time school nurse is unavailable. Most parents specifically recommend that teachers, coaches, and gym teachers receive diabetes care training alongside nurses to ensure comprehensive support. Regarding guidelines, the study emphasizes following established pediatric treatment standards that recommend individualizing blood glucose targets to reduce glucose variability and improve glycemic control throughout the school day.
passage_2: Care of Young Children With Diabetes in the Childcare and Community Setting: A Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the unique diabetes management needs, developmental factors, and legal protections for young children (aged 5 years and under) with diabetes—primarily type 1—within childcare and community settings. The paper finds that type 1 diabetes incidence is rising in young children who depend entirely on adults for daily care, while also noting that many families face unlawful discrimination, such as daycare refusal or expulsion due to blanket "no medication" policies. To address these challenges, the document outlines guidelines and recommendations centered on proactive, individualized care plans, stating that childcare programs are covered by federal antidiscrimination laws (such as the Americans with Disabilities Act) and must provide reasonable accommodations—including having trained, non-clinical staff available to monitor glucose levels, administer insulin and glucagon, and manage hyper- or hypoglycemia—while recommending a target HbA1c of <7% (or 7.5% for very young children) alongside collaborative partnerships between healthcare providers, parents, and childcare staff to ensure safe transitions and optimal health outcomes.
passage_3: The Hvidoere Childhood Diabetes Study Group Centre Differences Study 2005 evaluates the glycaemic targets set by diabetes teams, how these targets are perceived by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their parents, and their overall influence on metabolic control across 21 international centres. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

passage_1: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

However, a quantitative overview of all associated auto-immune diseases and their prevalence in T1D is lacking. Furthermore, random-effects meta-regression analysis was performed to assess the association between prevalence and mean age or diabetes duration. Results One hundred eighty articles were eligible including a total of 293 889 type 1 diabetes patients. Hypothyroidism (65 studies) was prevalent in 9.8% (95% CI: 7.5-12.3) of patients. Meta-regression showed that for every 10-year age increase, hypothyroidism prevalence increased 4.6% (95% CI: 2.6-6.6, P < 0.000, 54 studies). Weighted prevalence of celiac disease was 4.5% (95% CI: 4.0-5.5, 87 studies). Gastric autoimmunity was found in 4.3% of patients (95% CI: 1.6-8.2, 8 studies) and vitiligo in 2.4% (95% CI: 1.2-3.9, 14 studies) of patients. The prevalence of adrenal insufficiency was 0.2% (95% CI: 0.0-0.4, 14 studies) and hyperthyroidism was found in 1.3 percent (95% CI: 0.9-1.8, 45 studies) of type 1 diabetes patients. For all analyses, statistical heterogeneity between studies was moderate to high. Conclusions The prevalence of antibody-mediated auto-immune disease is high among type 1 diabetes patients. Especially hypothyroidism and celiac disease are frequently found.

Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.

The study analyzed 33 adolescent patients undergoing various procedures—including gastroplasty and standard, long-limb, or distal gastric bypass—and found that the operations resulted in significant, long-lasting weight loss alongside the resolution or marked improvement of major obesity-related comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea, hypertension, pseudotumor cerebri, and gastroesophageal reflux disease, while also substantially enhancing self-image and socialization without impairing physical or sexual maturation. Based on these findings, the paper supports offering bariatric surgery to severely obese adolescents who meet adult eligibility criteria, particularly when non-surgical treatments have failed, and recommends considering surgical intervention to prevent long-term health risks and social stigmatization despite current insurance coverage obstacles rooted in outdated consensus guidelines.

Another comparison group was adults undergoing gastric bypass at the same institution during the same time period. This report addresses the 2-year clinical outcome and five-year surgical adverse event rate. Body weight decreased from 133 kg (SD = 22) at inclusion to 92 kg (SD = 17) after 1 year and was 89 (SD = 18) after 2 years (p < 0·001) representing a 32% (-35 to -30) weight loss after 2 years, corresponding to 76% (-81 to -71) excess weight loss. Weight loss was similar in the adult gastric bypass patients (-31%) while weight gain (+3%) was seen in the conventionally treated obese adolescents. Significant improvement in cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors and inflammation was seen after surgery. The treatment was generally well tolerated and quality of life improved significantly. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. There were surgical complications similar to the adult group, which may be preventable.

question: What population was studied in the Behavioral Diabetes Social Ecological Perspectives for Pediatric and Adult Populations.txt study?
passage_1: Behavioral Diabetes: Social Ecological Perspectives for Pediatric and Adult Populations evaluates the complex interaction of psychosocial, behavioral, and ecological factors in managing diabetes across pediatric and adult age groups, emphasizing that optimal glycemic control relies heavily on addressing daily life stressors and psychological well-being alongside standard medical treatment. The text finds that psychosocial stressors significantly impact patient and family adherence to diabetes care routines, making behavioral support a critical component of effective disease management. To improve patient outcomes, it recommends integrating behaviorally oriented specialists into diabetes care teams and addressing the broader social and environmental contexts surrounding individuals with diabetes.
passage_2: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.
passage_3: Evidence-Based Behavioral Interventions to Promote Diabetes Management in Children, Adolescents, and Families evaluates contemporary psychological and behavioral interventions designed to support self-management, adherence, and health outcomes among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their families within key theoretical frameworks like Social Cognitive Theory, Family Systems Theory, and Social Ecological Models. Findings demonstrate that structured behavioral approaches—such as skills training, family-based teamwork, behavioral family systems therapy, and multi-systemic therapies—yield modest yet clinically meaningful improvements in regimen adherence, quality of life, and glycemic control, particularly when delivered early post-diagnosis, incorporating family collaboration, or targeting modifiable emotional and family processes rather than relying solely on education. Recommendations highlight tailoring behavioral interventions to meet the unique strengths and needs of individual families, evaluating cost-effectiveness for broader translation, combining mobile and digital health technologies with human contact, and conducting further culturally tailored research for youth with T2D. Finally, guidelines set by national and international diabetes organizations call for routine psychological screening and referral to evidence-based mental health therapies as standard components of pediatric clinical diabetes care.

Furthermore, key guidelines emphasized for ensuring patient safety include establishing carefully designed patient selection criteria, conducting multidisciplinary evaluations, choosing appropriate procedures, performing thorough screening and management of comorbidities, optimizing long-term compliance, and obtaining age-appropriate, fully informed consent.

The paper recommends managing adolescent bariatric surgery within a comprehensive, multidisciplinary team of pediatric specialists to address the unique medical, developmental, and psychosocial needs of young patients. Furthermore, it outlines clinical guidelines requiring candidates to have achieved most of their linear growth, have a BMI ≥40 with severe comorbidities or a BMI ≥50 with less severe comorbidities, and demonstrate the ability to commit to lifelong medical surveillance and dietary supplementation.

The guideline finds that pediatric obesity is a major global health concern driven by genetic susceptibilities in a permissive environment, noting that underlying endocrine etiologies are rare and typically accompanied by impaired growth velocity. For treatment and prevention, the guidelines recommend prescribing family-centered lifestyle modifications that emphasize nutrient-dense diets, limiting screen time to one to two hours per day, and participating in 20 to 60 minutes of daily physical activity. question: What were the main findings of the Celiac Disease in Children A Review of the Literature.txt review?
passage_1: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.
passage_2: "American College of Gastroenterology guidelines update: diagnosis and management of celiac disease" guideline presents an update to the 2013 American College of Gastroenterology Guideline on the Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease with updated recommendations for the evaluation and management of patients with celiac disease (CD). CD is defined as a permanent immune-mediated response to gluten present in wheat, barley, and rye. CD has a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations that resemble a multisystemic disorder rather than an isolated intestinal disease, and is characterized by small bowel injury and the presence of specific antibodies. Detection of CD-specific antibodies (e.g., tissue transglutaminase) in the serum is very helpful for the initial screening of patients with suspicion of CD. Intestinal biopsy is required in most patients to confirm the diagnosis. A nonbiopsy strategy for the diagnosis of CD in selected children is suggested and discussed in detail. Current treatment for CD requires strict adherence to a gluten-free diet (GFD) and lifelong medical follow-up. Most patients have excellent clinical response to a GFD. Nonresponsive CD is defined by persistent or recurrent symptoms despite being on a GFD. These patients require a systematic workup to rule out specific conditions that may cause persistent or recurrent symptoms, especially unintentional gluten contamination. Refractory CD is a rare cause of nonresponsive CD often associated with poor prognosis.
passage_3: "Screening for coeliac disease in type 1 diabetes" reports that the average prevalence of coeliac disease among children with diabetes mellitus in 26 reports was 4.5% (0.97-16.4%). Malabsorption, unstable diabetes, and growth failure, indicate that coeliac disease may be present. Even those who are apparently asymptomatic may have subtle complaints indicative of coeliac disease if a careful history is taken. Ill health may only be recognised in retrospect following the benefits conferred by a gluten free diet. For these reasons it is recommended that a screening programme should be instituted to detect coeliac disease in these children. Parents and where possible children themselves, should be fully involved at all stages of the screening, diagnostic, and treatment process.

Early diagnosis of celiac disease is very important to prevent long-term complications. Currently, the only effective treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet. In this review, we will discuss the epidemiology, clinical findings, diagnostic tests, and treatment of celiac disease in the light of the latest literature.

question: How did outcomes differ by sex/gender in the Celiac Disease in Children A Review of the Literature.txt review?
passage_1: "Sex- and age-dependent effects of celiac disease on growth and weight gain in children with type 1 diabetes: analysis of the Type 1 Diabetes Exchange Clinic Registry" reports that celiac disease (CD) is common in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and effects of CD on growth in children with T1D remain unclear. We analyzed heights, weights, and body mass index (BMI) in 215 matched pediatric CD/control pairs in the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry. CD was defined by a clinic-reported diagnosis and positive celiac serology (n = 80) and/or positive small bowel biopsy (n = 135). Cases and controls were matched by age (mean: 14 years), diabetes duration (median: 7 years), sex (57% female), and clinic site. There were 5569 height/weight measurements. Gluten was restricted for varying periods of time in 61% of females and 51% of males with CD. Females with CD were shorter than female controls at all ages (P = 0.01). Weight z-scores were initially lower in preschool females with CD but similar to controls by middle childhood. Males with CD were initially shorter but adult heights were similar. Height in both sexes and weight in males were lower in CD participants diagnosed at younger age. Growth in T1D children with biopsy-proven CD, 76% of them were gluten-restricted, was comparable to that of T1D controls. We concluded that concurrent CD impairs linear growth in T1D females at all stages of development and in young T1D males. Young females with CD have lower weights, but both sexes have similar weights by middle childhood. Children younger at CD onset remain shorter throughout childhood; males younger at CD onset have persistently lower weights. Long-term gluten restriction may restore weight gain and linear growth in children with CD and T1D.
passage_2: "Celiac disease in children with type 1 diabetes varies around the world: an international, cross-sectional study of 57 375 patients from the SWEET registry" reports that children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at much higher risk of developing celiac disease (CD) than the general population. The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). Further, they had lower glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in Europe and North America/Canada; lower body mass index (BMI)-SD score (BMI-SDS) in southern Europe, North America, and Canada; In most regions daily insulin dose was lower, height-SDS was lower, and the percentage of insulin pump users was higher in children with T1D and CD. We concluded that the prevalence and the anthropometric and metabolic consequences of CD in children with T1D differ around the world.
passage_3: "Younger age at onset and sex predict celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: an Italian multicenter study" estimates the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in Italian children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and to assess whether age at onset of type 1 diabetes is independently associated with diagnosis of celiac disease. The study group was a clinic-based cohort of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes cared for in 25 Italian centers for childhood diabetes. Yearly screening for celiac disease was performed using IgA/IgG anti-gliadin and IgA anti-endomysium antibodies. Of the 4,322 children and adolescents (age 11.8 ± 4.2 years) identified with type 1 diabetes, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was diagnosed in 292 (prevalence 6.8%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–7.6), with a higher risk seen in girls than in boys (odds ratio [OR] 1.93, 1.51–2.47). In 89% of these, diabetes was diagnosed before celiac disease. In logistic regression analyses, being younger at onset of diabetes, being female, and having a diagnosis of a thyroid disorder were independently associated with the risk of having diabetes and celiac disease. In comparison with subjects who were older than 9 years at onset of diabetes, subjects who were younger than 4 years at onset had an OR of 3.27 (2.20–4.85). We have provided evidence that 1) the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes is high (6.8%); 2) the risk of having both diseases is threefold higher in children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age <4 years than in those age >9 years; and 3) girls have a higher risk of having both diseases than boys.

question: What were the main findings of the Celiac Disease in Children With Type 1 Diabetes Varies Around the World An International Cross Sectional Study of 57375 Patients From the SWEET Registry.txt cross-sectional study?
passage_1: "Celiac disease in children with type 1 diabetes varies around the world: an international, cross-sectional study of 57 375 patients from the SWEET registry" reports that children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at much higher risk of developing celiac disease (CD) than the general population. The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). Further, they had lower glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in Europe and North America/Canada; lower body mass index (BMI)-SD score (BMI-SDS) in southern Europe, North America, and Canada; In most regions daily insulin dose was lower, height-SDS was lower, and the percentage of insulin pump users was higher in children with T1D and CD. We concluded that the prevalence and the anthropometric and metabolic consequences of CD in children with T1D differ around the world.

We analyzed heights, weights, and body mass index (BMI) in 215 matched pediatric CD/control pairs in the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry. CD was defined by a clinic-reported diagnosis and positive celiac serology (n = 80) and/or positive small bowel biopsy (n = 135). Cases and controls were matched by age (mean: 14 years), diabetes duration (median: 7 years), sex (57% female), and clinic site. There were 5569 height/weight measurements. Gluten was restricted for varying periods of time in 61% of females and 51% of males with CD. Females with CD were shorter than female controls at all ages (P = 0.01). Weight z-scores were initially lower in preschool females with CD but similar to controls by middle childhood. Males with CD were initially shorter but adult heights were similar. Height in both sexes and weight in males were lower in CD participants diagnosed at younger age. Growth in T1D children with biopsy-proven CD, 76% of them were gluten-restricted, was comparable to that of T1D controls. We concluded that concurrent CD impairs linear growth in T1D females at all stages of development and in young T1D males. Young females with CD have lower weights, but both sexes have similar weights by middle childhood. Children younger at CD onset remain shorter throughout childhood; males younger at CD onset have persistently lower weights. Long-term gluten restriction may restore weight gain and linear growth in children with CD and T1D.
passage_3: "Younger age at onset and sex predict celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: an Italian multicenter study" estimates the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in Italian children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and to assess whether age at onset of type 1 diabetes is independently associated with diagnosis of celiac disease. The study group was a clinic-based cohort of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes cared for in 25 Italian centers for childhood diabetes. Yearly screening for celiac disease was performed using IgA/IgG anti-gliadin and IgA anti-endomysium antibodies. Of the 4,322 children and adolescents (age 11.8 ± 4.2 years) identified with type 1 diabetes, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was diagnosed in 292 (prevalence 6.8%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–7.6), with a higher risk seen in girls than in boys (odds ratio [OR] 1.93, 1.51–2.47). In 89% of these, diabetes was diagnosed before celiac disease. In logistic regression analyses, being younger at onset of diabetes, being female, and having a diagnosis of a thyroid disorder were independently associated with the risk of having diabetes and celiac disease. In comparison with subjects who were older than 9 years at onset of diabetes, subjects who were younger than 4 years at onset had an OR of 3.27 (2.20–4.85). We have provided evidence that 1) the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes is high (6.8%); 2) the risk of having both diseases is threefold higher in children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age <4 years than in those age >9 years; and 3) girls have a higher risk of having both diseases than boys.

question: What were the main findings of the Characteristics of adolescents and youth with recent-onset type 2 diabetes the TODAY cohort at baseline.txt study?
passage_1: The “Characteristics of adolescents and youth with recent-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY cohort at baseline” evaluates the baseline demographic, clinical, medical history, and biochemical characteristics of 704 American adolescents and youth aged 10 to 17 years who were diagnosed with recent-onset type 2 diabetes for less than two years and had a body mass index at or above the 85th percentile. The findings reveal that the participant group was predominantly female (64.9%), had a mean age of 14.0 years, and consisted mostly of racial and ethnic minority populations, including 41.1% Hispanic and 31.5% non-Hispanic Black youth, with 89.4% having a family history of diabetes and significant socioeconomic challenges such as 41.5% residing in households earning less than $25,000 annually. Furthermore, clinical and biochemical comorbidities were highly prevalent within two years of diagnosis, including low high-density lipoprotein levels in 79.8%, blood pressure at or above the 90th percentile in 26.3%, microalbuminuria in 13.0%, and elevated triglycerides in 10.2% of participants. The study does not explicitly provide formal clinical practice guidelines or recommendations, but it emphasizes that youth-onset type 2 diabetes presents with substantial risk factors and metabolic abnormalities early in the course of the disease.
passage_2: “Retinopathy in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes Participating in the TODAY Clinical Trial” evaluates the prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in a cohort of 517 youth (aged 10–17 years at baseline) with type 2 diabetes of 2 to 8 years duration using standardized central grading of fundus photographs. The study found an overall retinopathy prevalence of 13.7%, with all affected participants exhibiting mild or very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and no cases of macular edema or proliferative disease. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. Although specific clinical recommendations and guidelines were not provided, the authors note that the natural history and progression of diabetic retinopathy in youth with type 2 diabetes will be further clarified through continued follow-up of this cohort.
passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

question: What were the main findings of the Comparison of Surgical and Medical Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes in Severely Obese Adolescents.txt study?
passage_1: "Comparison of Surgical and Medical Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes in Severely Obese Adolescents" evaluates the two-year outcomes of glycemic control, body mass index, blood pressure, lipid profiles, kidney function, and clinical adverse events in severely obese adolescents with type 2 diabetes undergoing bariatric surgery compared to those receiving medical therapy. The study found that surgical intervention led to a significant decrease in mean hemoglobin A1c concentration from 6.8% to 5.5% and a 29% reduction in body mass index, accompanied by marked improvements in blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and kidney function, whereas medical therapy resulted in increased hemoglobin A1c from 6.4% to 7.8%, a 3.7% increase in body mass index, and worsening or unchanged risk factors, though 23% of surgical patients required subsequent operations for complications. Based on these findings, the paper recommends conducting a well-designed, prospective controlled study to further define the precise role, long-term health, and surgical outcomes of metabolic surgery for adolescents with type 2 diabetes.
passage_2: "Metabolic Surgery in the Treatment Algorithm for Type 2 Diabetes: A Joint Statement by International Diabetes Organizations" evaluates the role, efficacy, and clinical indications of bariatric/metabolic surgery as an intervention for managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) alongside traditional medical and lifestyle therapies. The study findings demonstrate that gastrointestinal metabolic surgery achieves superior, durable glycemic control and significant reduction of cardiovascular risk factors compared to standard medical interventions. Based on these insights, the guidelines recommend metabolic surgery as a standard treatment option for T2D in candidates with class III obesity BMI≥40 kg/m² regardless of glycemic control, as well as for patients with class II obesity BMI 35.0-39.9 kg/m² when hyperglycemia is inadequately controlled by optimal medical therapy. Additionally, the guidelines state that surgery should be considered for patients with class I obesity BMI 30.0-34.9 kg/m² who experience inadequate control despite oral or injectable medications, noting that all specified BMI thresholds should be lowered by 2.5 kg/m² for patients of Asian descent. Finally, the recommendations emphasize performing operations in high-volume, multidisciplinary centers with long-term post-operative nutritional monitoring and urge healthcare regulators to update reimbursement policies to accommodate surgical diabetes care.
passage_3: "Impact of insulin and metformin versus metformin alone on β-cell function in youth with impaired glucose tolerance or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes" reported that pediatric type 2 diabetes prevalence is increasing, with β-cell dysfunction key in its pathogenesis. The RISE Pediatric Medication Study compared two approaches-glargine followed by metformin and metformin alone-in preserving or improving β-cell function in youth with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes during and after therapy withdrawal. Ninety-one pubertal, overweight/obese 10-19-year-old youth with IGT (60%) or type 2 diabetes of <6 months duration (40%) were randomized to either 3 months of insulin glargine with a target glucose of 4.4-5.0 mmol/L followed by 9 months of metformin or to 12 months of metformin alone. β-Cell function (insulin sensitivity paired with β-cell responses) was assessed by hyperglycemic clamp at baseline, 12 months (on treatment), and 15 months (3 months off treatment). No significant differences were observed between treatment groups at baseline, 12 months, or 15 months in β-cell function, BMI percentile, HbA1c, fasting glucose, or oral glucose tolerance test 2-h glucose results. In both treatment groups, clamp-measured β-cell function was significantly lower at 12 and 15 months versus baseline. HbA1c fell transiently at 6 months within both groups. BMI was higher in the glargine followed by metformin versus metformin alone group between 3 and 9 months. Only 5% of participants discontinued the interventions, and both treatments were well tolerated. We concluded that in youth with IGT or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, neither 3 months of glargine followed by 9 months of metformin nor 12 months of metformin alone halted the progressive deterioration of β-cell function. Alternate approaches to preserve β-cell function in youth are needed.
