By synthesizing evidence from a systematic literature search across biomedical databases, the review highlights that dietary protein significantly contributes to postprandial glycemic excursions alongside carbohydrates, leading to delayed hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the paper discusses recommendations and clinical guidelines to consider dietary protein composition—not just carbohydrate content alone—when calculating mealtime insulin doses to improve overall postprandial glycemic control.

question: What were the main findings of the Is exercise a therapeutic tool for improvement of cardiovascular risk factors in adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus A randomised controlled trial.txt study?
passage_1: The study “Is exercise a therapeutic tool for improvement of cardiovascular risk factors in adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus? A randomised controlled trial” is a therapeutic tool for improvement of cardiovascular risk factors in adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus? A randomised controlled trial evaluates the impact of a six-month exercise program on glycemic control, plasma lipid levels, blood pressure, hypoglycemia frequency, anthropometric measurements, and insulin requirements among 196 adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus. The findings reveal that regular exercise significantly improves glycemic control by reducing HbA1c levels, decreases dyslipidemia (lowering total cholesterol, LDL-C, and triglycerides while increasing HDL-C), reduces daily insulin dosage requirements, and leads to beneficial reductions in body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference without increasing the frequency of hypoglycemic attacks. Based on these results, the paper concludes and recommends that exercise should be considered an indispensable therapeutic component in the medical management of adolescents with type 1 diabetes to optimize glycemic control and mitigate cardiovascular risk factors.
passage_2: The study titled Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Physical Activity in Pediatric Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis evaluates the magnitude, precision, and constancy of differences in cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and daily physical activity levels between children/adolescents aged 18 years or younger with type 1 diabetes (T1D) or type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their peers without diabetes. Across a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, the authors found that cardiorespiratory fitness was significantly lower in youth with T2D (44.5% lower; SMD −1.06) and T1D (10% lower; SMD −0.39) compared to controls, with the deficits in CRF being much larger and more consistent among those with T2D. Daily physical activity was found to be marginally lower in youth with T1D (8.3% to 10% lower; SMD −0.29) and not significantly different in youth with T2D overall (SMD −0.56), though restricting analysis to strictly objective measurement tools revealed significantly reduced physical activity levels in both T2D (SMD −0.71) and T1D (SMD −0.67) groups compared to controls. Based on these findings, the paper highlights an increased risk for future cardiovascular disease-related morbidity in youth with diabetes—particularly those with T2D—and recommends the development of novel behavioral interventions designed to empower affected youth to engage in regular physical activity and improve their cardiorespiratory fitness.
passage_3: "Liraglutide in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes" reported that metformin is the regulatory-approved treatment of choice for most youth with type 2 diabetes early in the disease. However, early loss of glycemic control has been observed with metformin monotherapy. Whether liraglutide added to metformin (with or without basal insulin treatment) is safe and effective in youth with type 2 diabetes is unknown. Patients who were 10 to less than 17 years of age were randomly assigned, in a 1:1 ratio, to receive subcutaneous liraglutide (up to 1.8 mg per day) or placebo for a 26-week double-blind period, followed by a 26-week open-label extension period. Inclusion criteria were a body-mass index greater than the 85th percentile and a glycated hemoglobin level between 7.0 and 11.0% if the patients were being treated with diet and exercise alone or between 6.5 and 11.0% if they were being treated with metformin (with or without insulin). All the patients received metformin during the trial. The primary end point was the change from baseline in the glycated hemoglobin level after 26 weeks. Secondary end points included the change in fasting plasma glucose level. Safety was assessed throughout the course of the trial. Of 135 patients who underwent randomization, 134 received at least one dose of liraglutide (66 patients) or placebo (68 patients). Demographic characteristics were similar in the two groups (mean age, 14.6 years). At the 26-week analysis of the primary efficacy end point, the mean glycated hemoglobin level had decreased by 0.64 percentage points with liraglutide and increased by 0.42 percentage points with placebo, for an estimated treatment difference of -1.06 percentage points (P<0.001); the difference increased to -1.30 percentage points by 52 weeks. The fasting plasma glucose level had decreased at both time points in the liraglutide group but had increased in the placebo group.

passage_1: "Laparoscopic Gastric Banding in Morbidly Obese Adolescents" evaluates whether laparoscopic adjustable silicone gastric banding (LAGB) is a safe and effective weight loss method for morbidly obese adolescents. In this prospective study of 17 patients with a median age of 17 years followed over a median of 25 months, body mass index fell from a median of 44.7 to 30.2 kg/m² at 24 months, with patients achieving a median excess weight loss of 59.3%, 76.5% losing at least 50% of their excess weight, and only two complications reported (one slipped band and one leaking port). The study concludes that LAGB is a safe and effective medium-term weight loss treatment for morbidly obese adolescents, though its role in preventing adult obesity and related diseases requires further long-term study.
passage_2: "Surgery for the treatment of obesity in children and adolescents" evaluates the effectiveness and safety of surgical interventions compared to non-surgical lifestyle programs for managing obesity in children and adolescents under 18 years of age. Based on a single randomized controlled trial involving 50 Australian adolescents over two years, the study found that laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding resulted in a significantly greater mean weight reduction of 34.6 kg (a BMI change of 12.7) compared to a 3.0 kg reduction (a BMI change of 1.3) in the lifestyle intervention group, alongside minor improvements in physical functioning and health perception quality-of-life scores. However, adverse events were frequent, occurring in 48% of the surgical group—with 28% requiring revisional surgery due to complications—compared to 44% in the lifestyle group. The authors conclude that there is currently insufficient low-bias evidence to form definitive clinical guidelines, recommending that future research conduct larger high-quality randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up into adulthood to properly assess efficacy across diverse populations and identify post-operative care strategies that minimize complications and revision rates.
passage_3: "Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in adolescents with morbid obesity–surgical aspects and clinical outcome" addresses surgical aspects on bariatric surgery in adolescents from a nationwide Swedish study. Laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery was performed for 81 adolescents with morbid obesity (13-18 years), while 81 adolescents with obesity-matched by age, sex, and BMI received conventional care. Another comparison group was adults undergoing gastric bypass at the same institution during the same time period. This report addresses the 2-year clinical outcome and five-year surgical adverse event rate. Body weight decreased from 133 kg (SD = 22) at inclusion to 92 kg (SD = 17) after 1 year and was 89 (SD = 18) after 2 years (p < 0·001) representing a 32% (-35 to -30) weight loss after 2 years, corresponding to 76% (-81 to -71) excess weight loss. Weight loss was similar in the adult gastric bypass patients (-31%) while weight gain (+3%) was seen in the conventionally treated obese adolescents. Significant improvement in cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors and inflammation was seen after surgery. The treatment was generally well tolerated and quality of life improved significantly. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. There were surgical complications similar to the adult group, which may be preventable.

question: What population was studied in the Laparoscopic Roux en Y Gastric Bypass in Adolescents With Morbid Obesity Surgical Aspects and Clinical Outcome.txt study?
passage_1: "Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in adolescents with morbid obesity–surgical aspects and clinical outcome" addresses surgical aspects on bariatric surgery in adolescents from a nationwide Swedish study. Laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery was performed for 81 adolescents with morbid obesity (13-18 years), while 81 adolescents with obesity-matched by age, sex, and BMI received conventional care. Another comparison group was adults undergoing gastric bypass at the same institution during the same time period. This report addresses the 2-year clinical outcome and five-year surgical adverse event rate. Body weight decreased from 133 kg (SD = 22) at inclusion to 92 kg (SD = 17) after 1 year and was 89 (SD = 18) after 2 years (p < 0·001) representing a 32% (-35 to -30) weight loss after 2 years, corresponding to 76% (-81 to -71) excess weight loss. Weight loss was similar in the adult gastric bypass patients (-31%) while weight gain (+3%) was seen in the conventionally treated obese adolescents. Significant improvement in cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors and inflammation was seen after surgery. The treatment was generally well tolerated and quality of life improved significantly. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. There were surgical complications similar to the adult group, which may be preventable.
passage_2: "Teen-Longitudinal Assessment of Bariatric Surgery (Teen-LABS): Methodologic Features of the First Prospective Multicenter Study of Adolescent Bariatric Surgery" evaluates the methodological design and protocol of the first prospective, multicenter observational study designed to collect coordinated clinical, epidemiological, and behavioral data on adolescents (≤19 years old) undergoing bariatric surgery compared to adult historical counterparts. The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.
passage_3: "Surgery for the treatment of obesity in children and adolescents" evaluates the effectiveness and safety of surgical interventions compared to non-surgical lifestyle programs for managing obesity in children and adolescents under 18 years of age. Based on a single randomized controlled trial involving 50 Australian adolescents over two years, the study found that laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding resulted in a significantly greater mean weight reduction of 34.6 kg (a BMI change of 12.7) compared to a 3.0 kg reduction (a BMI change of 1.3) in the lifestyle intervention group, alongside minor improvements in physical functioning and health perception quality-of-life scores. However, adverse events were frequent, occurring in 48% of the surgical group—with 28% requiring revisional surgery due to complications—compared to 44% in the lifestyle group. The authors conclude that there is currently insufficient low-bias evidence to form definitive clinical guidelines, recommending that future research conduct larger high-quality randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up into adulthood to properly assess efficacy across diverse populations and identify post-operative care strategies that minimize complications and revision rates.

The study found that while limitations prevented direct comparisons of adult care visits with the control group, 78% of the intervention group participants discharged from pediatric care successfully established adult care visits, and the intervention group demonstrated significantly improved glycemic control, a lower incidence of severe hypoglycemia, and better global well-being compared to the control group.

question: What were the main findings of the Lipid profile and nutritional intake in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes improve after a structured dietician training to a Mediterranean-style diet.txt study?
passage_1: “Lipid profile and nutritional intake in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes improve after a structured dietician training to a Mediterranean-style diet” evaluates nutritional intakes and lipid profiles in 96 children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes before and after a six-month structured dietician training program to a Mediterranean-style diet. The study finds that at baseline, participants consumed a generally balanced diet but had excessive fat intake and low dietary fiber intake, resulting in a high rate of abnormal lipid profiles where 64.5% and 29.1% of subjects exceeded the 75th and 95th percentiles for lipid risk parameters, respectively; following the six-month intervention, daily fat and cholesterol intake significantly decreased while fiber intake increased, leading to statistically significant reductions in LDL-cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and total cholesterol to HDL-cholesterol ratios independently of body weight and glycemic control (HbA_1c). Based on these findings, the paper recommends incorporating structured, dietician-led nutritional training focused on a Mediterranean-style diet into standard pediatric diabetes management to optimize dietary quality and lower long-term cardiovascular risk factors.

A randomised controlled trial evaluates the impact of a six-month exercise program on glycemic control, plasma lipid levels, blood pressure, hypoglycemia frequency, anthropometric measurements, and insulin requirements among 196 adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus. The findings reveal that regular exercise significantly improves glycemic control by reducing HbA1c levels, decreases dyslipidemia (lowering total cholesterol, LDL-C, and triglycerides while increasing HDL-C), reduces daily insulin dosage requirements, and leads to beneficial reductions in body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference without increasing the frequency of hypoglycemic attacks. Based on these results, the paper concludes and recommends that exercise should be considered an indispensable therapeutic component in the medical management of adolescents with type 1 diabetes to optimize glycemic control and mitigate cardiovascular risk factors.

Analyzing 18 randomized controlled trials, the study found that neither physical activity alone nor nutrition-based interventions alone produced statistically significant reductions in HbA1c levels compared to control groups, though results generally trended favorably toward enhancing glycemic control and quality of life, with initial evidence from a single hybrid study showing promise for multi-component interventions. Based on these findings, the study recommend further research with larger, high-quality trials to establish concrete guidelines and better understand the long-term potential of structured lifestyle and combined hybrid interventions for pediatric T1DM management.

The paper finds that the atherosclerotic process begins during childhood, progresses faster when compounded by high low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and additional cardiovascular risk factors, and that statin therapy can safely and effectively reverse early vascular structural and functional abnormalities in young patients. Based on these findings, the guidelines recommend targeted screening using family history and fasting lipid profiles, with initial management prioritizing six to twelve months of dietary and lifestyle modifications. Synthesizing evidence from landmark studies like Bogalusa and PDAY, the report finds that atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease begins in childhood, tracks into adulthood, and is exacerbated by early risk factors like high LDL, low HDL, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome. To address these risks, the paper recommends a targeted screening strategy using fasting lipid profiles for children and adolescents with a positive family history of premature cardiovascular disease or high cholesterol, as well as for those with unknown family histories or co-occurring risk factors like obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. The guidelines emphasize cardiovascular disease prevention through lifestyle modifications—specifically adhering to the Dietary Guidelines for Americans and increasing daily physical activity—while introducing updated recommendations for pharmacologic treatment, such as statin therapy, for children with severe dyslipidemia who fail lifestyle intervention.

While intensive lifestyle intervention yielded lower triglyceride levels and rosiglitazone co-treatment reduced hsCRP compared to metformin alone, standard glucose-lowering treatments and protocol-driven statin adjustments were generally inadequate to arrest this worsening risk, leading to the paper's main recommendation and guideline implication that standard diabetes treatments are insufficient on their own and that aggressive, dedicated management of dyslipidemia and inflammatory risk factors is critical for youth with type 2 diabetes.

Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.
passage_2: Longitudinal Trends in Glycemic Outcomes and Technology Use for Over 48,000 People with Type 1 Diabetes (2016–2022) from the T1D Exchange Quality Improvement Collaborative evaluates longitudinal trends in glycemic control (HbA1c) and diabetes technology adoption across more than 48,000 individuals with type 1 diabetes, stratified by race/ethnicity and insurance status. The findings show an overall clinically significant improvement in average HbA1c levels from 8.7% in 2016–2017 to 8.4% in 2021–2022, accompanied by a rise in participants reaching target HbA1c levels (<7%) from 20% to 26% and a decrease in those with severe hyperglycemia (>9%) from 43% to 31%. Alongside these glycemic gains, the uptake of diabetes technology increased significantly across continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and hybrid closed-loop systems; however, pronounced health inequities persisted, as non-Hispanic White and privately insured individuals consistently maintained better glycemic outcomes and higher device adoption rates than non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and publicly insured patients. Based on these insights, the study highlights the need for targeted quality improvement interventions, policy adjustments, and funded research to directly address socio-behavioral barriers and ensure equitable access to diabetes technology and care across diverse populations.

passage_1: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.
passage_2: Longitudinal Trends in Glycemic Outcomes and Technology Use for Over 48,000 People with Type 1 Diabetes (2016–2022) from the T1D Exchange Quality Improvement Collaborative evaluates longitudinal trends in glycemic control (HbA1c) and diabetes technology adoption across more than 48,000 individuals with type 1 diabetes, stratified by race/ethnicity and insurance status. The findings show an overall clinically significant improvement in average HbA1c levels from 8.7% in 2016–2017 to 8.4% in 2021–2022, accompanied by a rise in participants reaching target HbA1c levels (<7%) from 20% to 26% and a decrease in those with severe hyperglycemia (>9%) from 43% to 31%. Alongside these glycemic gains, the uptake of diabetes technology increased significantly across continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and hybrid closed-loop systems; however, pronounced health inequities persisted, as non-Hispanic White and privately insured individuals consistently maintained better glycemic outcomes and higher device adoption rates than non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and publicly insured patients. Based on these insights, the study highlights the need for targeted quality improvement interventions, policy adjustments, and funded research to directly address socio-behavioral barriers and ensure equitable access to diabetes technology and care across diverse populations.

passage_1: The “Health-Related Quality of Life of Children and Adolescents with Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus” evaluates the associations between demographic and diabetes management variables and the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) among 2,445 children and adolescents aged 8 to 22 years with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus across multiple U.S. study sites. The study found that youth with type 2 diabetes reported significantly lower overall HRQOL compared to those with type 1 diabetes; among participants with type 1 diabetes, worse HRQOL was associated with government-funded insurance, insulin injections versus pump therapy, elevated HbA_1c levels (≥9%), higher rates of comorbidities, and recent emergency department visits or hospitalizations, alongside a significant age-by-sex interaction where HRQOL declined in older girls but improved in older boys. For participants with type 2 diabetes, injecting insulin at least three times daily was associated with better HRQOL, whereas having two or more emergency department visits in the preceding six months was associated with lower HRQOL. The authors recommend that interventions aimed at improving HRQOL in youth with diabetes account for treatment modal differences, complication risks, and gender-specific adjustment patterns across developmental age groups.
passage_2: "Transfer from paediatric to adult care for young adults with Type 2 diabetes: the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study" evaluates the factors associated with healthcare transfer and poor glycaemic control among young adults with Type 2 diabetes using data from the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study. The findings indicate that out of 182 participants, 56% transferred to adult care, 15% received no care, and 29% remained in pediatric care, with higher age at diagnosis and longer diabetes duration predicting the departure from pediatric care. Furthermore, transferring to adult care or receiving no care was significantly associated with higher odds of poor glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥ 9.0%), independent of sex, race, ethnicity, or baseline HbA1c levels. Recommendations and guidelines provided in the paper emphasize the urgent need for tailored clinical programs, healthcare system policies, targeted treatments, patient-centered care, and early education for both adult specialists and generalists to support the growing population of young adults with youth-onset Type 2 diabetes and prevent disease deterioration during the transition period.

Analyzing 927 participants from the Pediatric Diabetes Consortium, the authors found that African American participants, compared to non-Hispanic Whites, presented with higher body mass index percentiles, more advanced pubertal development, and a higher frequency of diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis—a disparity largely explained by socioeconomic factors like health insurance—while also experiencing higher rates of hypertension, severe hypoglycemia, higher HbA1c levels, higher required insulin doses, and lower rates of entering partial remission over three years. Similarly, Hispanic participants exhibited higher BMI percentiles at diagnosis and throughout follow-up, a higher prevalence of dyslipidemia, and sustained trajectories of higher insulin doses and IDAA1c compared to non-Hispanic Whites. question: What did the Management of Newly Diagnosed Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) in Children and Adolescents.txt clinical trial find regarding metformin?
passage_1: "A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes (TODAY)” study evaluates the efficacy of three treatment regimens—metformin alone, metformin combined with rosiglitazone, and metformin combined with an intensive lifestyle-intervention program—in achieving durable glycemic control among children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that metformin plus rosiglitazone was particularly effective in girls, while metformin monotherapy was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants. Serious adverse events occurred in 19.2% of participants across the trial, and although the paper does not explicitly state formal clinical recommendations or guidelines, it concludes that metformin monotherapy fails to maintain durable glycemic control in roughly half of youth with type 2 diabetes and that adding rosiglitazone provides superior glycemic durability compared to monotherapy or intensive lifestyle interventions.
passage_2: "Impact of insulin and metformin versus metformin alone on β-cell function in youth with impaired glucose tolerance or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes" reported that pediatric type 2 diabetes prevalence is increasing, with β-cell dysfunction key in its pathogenesis. The RISE Pediatric Medication Study compared two approaches-glargine followed by metformin and metformin alone-in preserving or improving β-cell function in youth with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes during and after therapy withdrawal. Ninety-one pubertal, overweight/obese 10-19-year-old youth with IGT (60%) or type 2 diabetes of <6 months duration (40%) were randomized to either 3 months of insulin glargine with a target glucose of 4.4-5.0 mmol/L followed by 9 months of metformin or to 12 months of metformin alone. β-Cell function (insulin sensitivity paired with β-cell responses) was assessed by hyperglycemic clamp at baseline, 12 months (on treatment), and 15 months (3 months off treatment). No significant differences were observed between treatment groups at baseline, 12 months, or 15 months in β-cell function, BMI percentile, HbA1c, fasting glucose, or oral glucose tolerance test 2-h glucose results. In both treatment groups, clamp-measured β-cell function was significantly lower at 12 and 15 months versus baseline. HbA1c fell transiently at 6 months within both groups. BMI was higher in the glargine followed by metformin versus metformin alone group between 3 and 9 months. Only 5% of participants discontinued the interventions, and both treatments were well tolerated. We concluded that in youth with IGT or recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, neither 3 months of glargine followed by 9 months of metformin nor 12 months of metformin alone halted the progressive deterioration of β-cell function. Alternate approaches to preserve β-cell function in youth are needed.
passage_3: "Management of Newly Diagnosed Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) in Children and Adolescents" evaluates evidence-based management strategies for patients aged 10 to 18 years diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus in response to rising childhood obesity rates. The paper's findings highlight that childhood type 2 diabetes disproportionately affects ethnic minority youth between 10 and 19 years old and notes a scarcity of pediatric-specific clinical trial data and educational resources for managing the condition in younger populations. To address this, the guidelines recommend initiating insulin therapy immediately for patients who present with ketosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, diagnostic uncertainty between type 1 and type 2 diabetes, severe hyperglycemia (random blood glucose ≥ 250 mg/dL), or an HbA1c > 9%, while recommending first-line treatment with metformin combined with lifestyle modifications for all other stable, non-ketotic patients. Additionally, the recommendations emphasize incorporating evidence-based pediatric weight management nutrition counsel, engaging in at least 60 minutes of daily moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, limiting nonacademic screen time to under 2 hours daily, monitoring HbA1c concentrations every 3 months, and conducting finger-stick blood glucose monitoring for patients who take hypoglycemia-risk medications, are adjusting regimens, experience intercurrent illness, or fail to meet target glycemic goals.

Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of T2DM in adults. The objective was to assess the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin in children and adolescents with T2DM. This was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03170518; EudraCT: 2016-005223-88) conducted at 104 sites in 10 countries. Participants were children and adolescents aged 10 years or older with T2DM (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] ≥6.5% to ≤11%). Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The treatment period was 52 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, along with secondary efficacy end points and safety. A total of 171 participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (n = 84) or placebo (n = 87). At week 26, HbA1c reduction from baseline was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (difference in least-squares means, -0.76% [95% CI, -1.25% to -0.27%]; P = 0.002). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). Treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) occurred in 77.4% and 74.7% and serious treatment-emergent AEs in 9.5% and 5.7% of participants who received canagliflozin and placebo, respectively.

This multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised phase 3 study was undertaken at 30 centres in five countries (Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Russia, and the USA). Participants aged 10-24 years with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c concentration of 6·5-11% (48-97 mmol/mol) were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo during a 24 week double-blind period, which was then followed by a 28 week open-label safety extension in which all participants received dapagliflozin. Participants and study personnel were masked and participants were randomly assigned treatment (placebo or study drug) using an interactive web and voice response system. The primary outcome was between-group differences in change in HbA1c concentration from baseline to 24 weeks (intention-to-treat analysis). The authors find that while classic inulin clearance remains the gold standard, its clinical utility is severely limited by assay complexity, poor availability, and the challenge of timed urine collections in young or functionally impaired children. Radioisotopes like (_^99"m" )"Tc-DTPA" and (_^125)"I-iothalamate" present measurement challenges or undergo tubular secretion, whereas creatinine-based estimates can falsely elevate GFR unless cimetidine is used to block tubular secretion. Ultimately, the paper recommends iohexol plasma disappearance as the optimal alternative, citing its exceptional safety profile, ease of measurement, lack of renal metabolism or tubular transport, and high correlation with multi-compartment disappearance models. Based on these findings, the study highlights guidelines for optimizing sampling protocols—such as using a streamlined four-point or five-point blood sampling schedule over at least 5 hours (or up to 24 hours in severe chronic kidney disease)—and suggests fingerprick blood spot sampling as a practical, scalable approach for outpatient and epidemiological GFR monitoring.

Based on these findings, the authors conclude that the combined creatinine–cystatin C equation performs superiorly to equations using either marker alone and recommend its use as a confirmatory test for chronic kidney disease.

question: What were the main findings of the Microvascular complications assessment in adolescents with 2- to 5-yr duration of type 1 diabetes from 1990 to 2006.txt study?
passage_1: The study titled "Microvascular complications assessment in adolescents with 2- to 5-yr duration of type 1 diabetes from 1990 to 2006" evaluates the prevalence trends and risk factors of early microvascular complications—specifically retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy—in 819 adolescents aged 11 to 17 years with 2 to 5 years of type 1 diabetes duration treated at a tertiary pediatric clinic over a 17-year period. The study found that early retinopathy declined significantly from 16% to 7% between 1990 and 2002 before plateauing, early indicators of nephropathy (elevated albumin excretion rate and microalbuminuria) remained stable over time, and peripheral nerve abnormalities increased from 14% to 23%, all occurring alongside improvements in median HbA1c and increased daily insulin injections. Based on the presence of early complications even within short diabetes durations, the paper supports clinical guidelines recommending that routine microvascular screening in pubertal children with type 1 diabetes commence after 2 years of disease duration.
passage_2: The study “Screening eye exams in youth with type 1 diabetes under 18 years of age: once may be enough?” evaluates the optimal frequency and necessity of eye screening examinations in pediatric patients under 18 years of age with type 1 diabetes, drawing on long-term data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) research group. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.
passage_3: “Retinopathy in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes Participating in the TODAY Clinical Trial” evaluates the prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in a cohort of 517 youth (aged 10–17 years at baseline) with type 2 diabetes of 2 to 8 years duration using standardized central grading of fundus photographs. The study found an overall retinopathy prevalence of 13.7%, with all affected participants exhibiting mild or very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and no cases of macular edema or proliferative disease. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. Although specific clinical recommendations and guidelines were not provided, the authors note that the natural history and progression of diabetic retinopathy in youth with type 2 diabetes will be further clarified through continued follow-up of this cohort.

The study found that 19.3% of participants endorsed elevated depressive symptoms, 18.9% of a subgroup with item-level data endorsed thoughts of self-harm, and higher depressive symptoms were significantly associated with older age, shorter diabetes duration, higher A1C levels, being non-Hispanic White, more frequent daily blood glucose checks, and oral medication use. Additionally, only 50% of those screening positive for elevated depressive symptoms had a documented mental health referral in their electronic health record. The authors highlight the need for improved processes regarding mental health service referrals, standardized documentation of symptoms and referrals in electronic health records, dedicated self-harm assessments, and expanded mental health resources for this population.

Based on these gaps, the authors recommend that future research focus on four key areas: including youth with diagnosed MDD, conducting treatment studies addressing both T2D and MDD concurrently, analyzing larger and more racially diverse youth samples, and evaluating how social determinants of health alongside mental health comorbidities impact T2D outcomes.

In a sample of 2,672 youth aged 10 to 21 years with a mean diabetes duration of 5 years, 14% exhibited mildly depressed mood (CES-D 16–23) and 8.6% exhibited moderately or severely depressed mood (CES-D ≥ 24), with overall prevalence rates comparable to published estimates for youth without diabetes. Females reported higher mean depression scores than males, and after adjusting for demographic factors and diabetes duration, depressed mood was found to be higher among males with type 2 diabetes than those with type 1 diabetes, as well as higher among females with comorbidities than those without. Higher mean HbA1c levels and higher frequency of emergency department visits were significantly associated with depressed mood, prompting the recommendation that physicians and healthcare professionals consider screening youth with diabetes for depressed mood in clinical settings, especially targeting youth with poor glycemic control, frequent emergency department visits, males with type 2 diabetes, and females with comorbidities.

question: What were the main findings of the NEJM 2012 study on estimating glomerular filtration rate (GFR) from serum creatinine and cystatin C.txt study?
passage_1: The “NEJM 2012 study on estimating glomerular filtration rate (GFR) from serum creatinine and cystatin C” evaluates the accuracy and clinical utility of new GFR estimating equations using standardized serum cystatin C alone and in combination with standardized serum creatinine across diverse populations. The study finds that while equations based on creatinine alone or cystatin C alone show similar bias and accuracy across estimated GFR ranges, the combined creatinine–cystatin C equation significantly improves precision and reduces estimation errors greater than 30%. Furthermore, in participants with a creatinine-based estimated GFR of 45 to 74 mL/min/1.73 m², the combined equation markedly improves the reclassification of measured GFR, correctly reclassifying 16.9% of those with a creatinine-based estimated GFR of 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m² as having a GFR of 60 mL/min/1.73 m² or higher. Based on these findings, the authors conclude that the combined creatinine–cystatin C equation performs superiorly to equations using either marker alone and recommend its use as a confirmatory test for chronic kidney disease.

The findings demonstrate that microalbuminuria developed at a rate of 3.3 per 100 person-years, with recent HbA1c levels (from the 1st and 2nd years preceding onset) serving as a stronger predictor of risk than older or cumulative 4-year measurements, indicating an attenuation of the impact of past hyperglycemia over time. The study identified a significant nonlinear relationship between HbA1c and microalbuminuria risk, showing a markedly steeper increase in risk once HbA1c exceeds 8%, a risk enhancement that is further magnified among current cigarette smokers (who experienced an incidence rate of 7.9 per 100 person-years compared to 1.8 for past smokers and 2.2 for never-smokers). While no explicit clinical guidelines or recommendations are formally established in the text, the authors conclude that patients with type 1 diabetes who smoke and maintain HbA1c levels above 8% face the highest risk for developing microalbuminuria.

Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of T2DM in adults. The objective was to assess the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin in children and adolescents with T2DM. This was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03170518; EudraCT: 2016-005223-88) conducted at 104 sites in 10 countries. Participants were children and adolescents aged 10 years or older with T2DM (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] ≥6.5% to ≤11%). Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The treatment period was 52 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, along with secondary efficacy end points and safety. A total of 171 participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (n = 84) or placebo (n = 87). At week 26, HbA1c reduction from baseline was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (difference in least-squares means, -0.76% [95% CI, -1.25% to -0.27%]; P = 0.002). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). Treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) occurred in 77.4% and 74.7% and serious treatment-emergent AEs in 9.5% and 5.7% of participants who received canagliflozin and placebo, respectively.

question: What were the main findings of the Neurological Consequences of Diabetic Ketoacidosis at Initial Presentation of Type 1 Diabetes in a Prospective Cohort Study of Children.txt cohort study?
passage_1: The study Neurological Consequences of Diabetic Ketoacidosis at Initial Presentation of Type 1 Diabetes in a Prospective Cohort Study of Children evaluates the acute and medium-term impacts of new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) on brain morphology and cognitive function in children newly diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes. By assessing children aged 6 to 18 years at baseline, day 5, day 28, and 6 months using MRI, MRS, and cognitive testing, the study highlights how DKA alters cerebral structure and neurocognitive performance even without the presence of severe clinical cerebral edema. The findings reveal that children presenting with DKA experience significant changes in white and gray matter structures, including higher total white matter volume and increased mean diffusivity in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes at presentation, alongside reduced total cortical gray matter volume and lower levels of N-acetylaspartate in the frontal gray matter and basal ganglia. Although acute structural and volume changes resolved over time, DKA presentation was associated with persistent adverse functional outcomes at the 6-month follow-up, specifically lower delayed memory recall, poorer sustained and divided attention, and reduced baseline mental state scores. Furthermore, lower blood pH at presentation and younger age were identified as key predictors of both structural brain changes and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. The recommendations and guidelines stemming from this study emphasize the critical need to view DKA-related brain injury along a continuous spectrum rather than as an isolated risk limited to overt cerebral edema. Clinicians and healthcare providers are urged to prioritize early detection and prompt intervention for Type 1 Diabetes in pediatric patients to prevent initial DKA episodes entirely, thereby protecting vulnerable developing brain tissue.

Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.

The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.

The study found that 46 patients (19.4%) had an NPD diagnosis—including depression, ADHD, neurodevelopmental disorders, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder—at the time of T2DM presentation, with no statistically significant differences in demographic characteristics or BMI between affected and unaffected groups, and that 63% of affected patients were taking psychotropic medications (most commonly mood stabilizers and atypical antipsychotics). Based on these findings, the paper suggests implications for establishing screening regimens for pediatric populations at high risk for T2DM and for guiding therapeutic interventions, including lifestyle measures.
passage_2: The study "Mental health comorbidity and youth onset type 2 diabetes: A systematic review of the literature" evaluates the current literature surrounding youth with depression and type 2 diabetes (T2D), specifically reviewing 13 publications from 8 studies involving 2,244 individuals aged 6 to 17. The findings indicate that while depressive symptoms are common in youth with T2D and correlate with negative T2D outcomes, most studies failed to formally assess for major depressive disorder (MDD) and actively excluded participants with a prior MDD diagnosis. Based on these gaps, the authors recommend that future research focus on four key areas: including youth with diagnosed MDD, conducting treatment studies addressing both T2D and MDD concurrently, analyzing larger and more racially diverse youth samples, and evaluating how social determinants of health alongside mental health comorbidities impact T2D outcomes.

The review finds that pediatric type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to the childhood obesity epidemic, peak incidence during puberty, and higher prevalence in specific high-risk ethnic groups (such as African-American, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and Native American populations), with many cases presenting asymptomatically or mild in severity. Based on these findings, the paper recommends targeted screening for overweight or obese youth aged 10 and older (or at pubertal onset) who possess additional risk factors like a family history of diabetes or signs of insulin resistance, utilizing fasting glucose, oral glucose tolerance testing, or HbA1c every two years. Finally, the study guidelines emphasize lifestyle intervention (diet and exercise) as the primary first-line treatment, supplemented by pharmacological therapy such as metformin when lifestyle modifications alone are insufficient, while highlighting the need to restructure healthcare delivery to improve long-term retention and care adherence among affected adolescents.

passage_1: The study Obesity in youth with type 1 diabetes in Germany, Austria, and the United States examined the prevalence of obesity among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) using data from two large pediatric clinical registries in the United States and Europe—the T1D Exchange (n = 11,435) and the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (n = 21,501). Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Furthermore, higher BMI z-scores were significantly associated with elevated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and a higher frequency of severe hypoglycemia across both groups, suggesting that obesity presents additional challenges to achieving optimal glycemic control in young individuals with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: "Obesity in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes in Germany, Austria, and the United States" examines the current extent of the obesity problem in 2 large pediatric clinical registries in the US and Europe and to examine the hypotheses that increased body mass index (BMI) z-scores (BMIz) are associated with greater hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and increased frequency of severe hypoglycemia in youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D), international (World Health Organization) and national (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/German Health Interview and Examination Survey for Children and Adolescents) BMI references were used to calculate BMIz in participants (age 2-<18 years and ≥ 1 year duration of T1D) enrolled in the T1D Exchange (n = 11,435) and the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (n = 21,501). Associations between BMIz and HbA1c and severe hypoglycemia were assessed. Participants in both registries had median BMI values that were greater than international and their respective national reference values. BMIz was significantly greater in the T1D Exchange vs the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (P < .001). After stratification by age-group, no differences in BMI between registries existed for children 2-5 years, but differences were confirmed for 6- to 9-, 10- to 13-, and 14- to 17-year age groups (all P < .001). Greater BMIz were significantly related to greater HbA1c levels and more frequent occurrence of severe hypoglycemia across the registries, although these associations may not be clinically relevant. We concluded that excessive weight is a common problem in children with T1D in Germany and Austria and, especially, in the US. Our data suggest that obesity contributes to the challenges in achieving optimal glycemic control in children and adolescents with T1D.

Among youth with type 2 diabetes, 79.4% were obese and 10.4% were overweight, while among those with type 1 diabetes, 12.6% were obese and 22.1% were overweight. Youth with type 1 diabetes had a higher prevalence of overweight than youth without diabetes (22.1% vs. 16.1%), although their overall obesity rate was not significantly higher. The findings highlight that obesity is particularly common among youth with type 2 diabetes, while overweight is also an important concern among youth with type 1 diabetes.

Consequently, the efficacy and safety of once-weekly injections of exenatide for the treatment of youth with type 2 diabetes was evaluated. Participants (aged 10 to <18 years) were randomized (5:2) to once-weekly exenatide 2 mg or placebo, respectively. Associations between BMIz and HbA1c and severe hypoglycemia were assessed. Participants in both registries had median BMI values that were greater than international and their respective national reference values. BMIz was significantly greater in the T1D Exchange vs the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (P < .001). After stratification by age-group, no differences in BMI between registries existed for children 2-5 years, but differences were confirmed for 6- to 9-, 10- to 13-, and 14- to 17-year age groups (all P < .001). Greater BMIz were significantly related to greater HbA1c levels and more frequent occurrence of severe hypoglycemia across the registries, although these associations may not be clinically relevant. We concluded that excessive weight is a common problem in children with T1D in Germany and Austria and, especially, in the US. Our data suggest that obesity contributes to the challenges in achieving optimal glycemic control in children and adolescents with T1D.
passage_2: The study Obesity in youth with type 1 diabetes in Germany, Austria, and the United States examined the prevalence of obesity among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) using data from two large pediatric clinical registries in the United States and Europe—the T1D Exchange (n = 11,435) and the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (n = 21,501). Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Furthermore, higher BMI z-scores were significantly associated with elevated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and a higher frequency of severe hypoglycemia across both groups, suggesting that obesity presents additional challenges to achieving optimal glycemic control in young individuals with type 1 diabetes.
passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

Analyzing 18 randomized controlled trials, the study found that neither physical activity alone nor nutrition-based interventions alone produced statistically significant reductions in HbA1c levels compared to control groups, though results generally trended favorably toward enhancing glycemic control and quality of life, with initial evidence from a single hybrid study showing promise for multi-component interventions. question: What were the main findings of the Physical Activity Exercise and Diabetes A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association.txt position statement?
passage_1: Physical Activity/Exercise and Diabetes: A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the evidence and clinical strategies regarding the role of physical activity and exercise in managing and preventing type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes, and prediabetes. It finds that regular physical activity improves insulin sensitivity, cardiorespiratory fitness, blood glucose control, and vascular health while lowering cardiovascular mortality risk in type 2 diabetes, whereas interrupting sedentary time reduces acute postprandial glucose spikes. The statement recommends that all adults, particularly those with type 2 diabetes, minimize prolonged sedentary behavior by stepping away from sitting every 30 minutes, and that adults with type 2 diabetes perform a combination of aerobic and resistance exercises without letting more than two consecutive days elapse between sessions. To prevent or delay type 2 diabetes onset in high-risk individuals, it recommends lifestyle interventions incorporating at least 150 minutes per week of physical activity and dietary modifications targeting 5% to 7% weight loss. Finally, for individual safety during physical activity, the guidelines specify checking blood glucose prior to exercise to maintain a target starting range between 90 mg/dL and 250 mg/dL, consuming 15–30 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates if glucose is under 90 mg/dL, and testing for ketones—avoiding exercise if moderate-to-large ketone levels are present—when blood glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL.
passage_2: "Metabolic Surgery in the Treatment Algorithm for Type 2 Diabetes: A Joint Statement by International Diabetes Organizations" evaluates the role, efficacy, and clinical indications of bariatric/metabolic surgery as an intervention for managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) alongside traditional medical and lifestyle therapies. The study findings demonstrate that gastrointestinal metabolic surgery achieves superior, durable glycemic control and significant reduction of cardiovascular risk factors compared to standard medical interventions. Based on these insights, the guidelines recommend metabolic surgery as a standard treatment option for T2D in candidates with class III obesity BMI≥40 kg/m² regardless of glycemic control, as well as for patients with class II obesity BMI 35.0-39.9 kg/m² when hyperglycemia is inadequately controlled by optimal medical therapy. Additionally, the guidelines state that surgery should be considered for patients with class I obesity BMI 30.0-34.9 kg/m² who experience inadequate control despite oral or injectable medications, noting that all specified BMI thresholds should be lowered by 2.5 kg/m² for patients of Asian descent. Finally, the recommendations emphasize performing operations in high-volume, multidisciplinary centers with long-term post-operative nutritional monitoring and urge healthcare regulators to update reimbursement policies to accommodate surgical diabetes care.
passage_3: Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement evaluates the neuroendocrine and metabolic responses to different modalities of physical activity—including aerobic, anaerobic, resistance, and high-intensity interval training—in individuals living with type 1 diabetes. The paper finds that while regular exercise offers substantial cardiometabolic benefits such as improved HbA1c, reduced cardiovascular risk, and enhanced fitness, blood glucose responses fluctuate widely depending on the type of activity, with aerobic exercise typically decreasing blood glucose and anaerobic or high-intensity exercise often causing glucose stability or transient hyperglycemia. To mitigate exercise barriers such as fear of hypoglycemia, the authors present guidelines recommending a target of 150 minutes of weekly physical activity for adults and 60 minutes daily for youth, alongside specific starting blood glucose targets (7–10 mmol/L for aerobic exercise lasting up to an hour, and 5–7 mmol/L for anaerobic or interval training). Furthermore, the statement provides practical recommendations on nutritional intake, insulin dose reductions before and after activity, and continuous glucose monitoring strategies to prevent exercise-related glucose excursions and nocturnal hypoglycemia.

Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Furthermore, higher BMI z-scores were significantly associated with elevated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and a higher frequency of severe hypoglycemia across both groups, suggesting that obesity presents additional challenges to achieving optimal glycemic control in young individuals with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: "Polyendocrinopathy in children, adolescents, and young adults with type 1 diabetes: a multicenter analysis of 28,671 patients from the German/Austrian DPV-Wiss database" investigates diabetes-specific autoantibodies and additional autoimmune phenomena in a large cohort of young patients with type 1 diabetes. Data from 28,671 patients <30 years with type 1 diabetes from 242 specialized centers in Germany and Austria were analyzed. At least one beta-cell antibody was present in 81.6% of patients. beta-cell-Ab-negative patients were significantly younger at diabetes onset (P < 0.0001). A total of 19.6% had positive thyroid antibodies with female predominance (62%, P < 0.0001). Antibodies to tissue transglutaminase were present in 10.7%, with a significantly longer duration of diabetes (P < 0.0001). Parietal cell antibodies were found in 283 patients, associated with older age (P < 0.001), and adrenal antibodies were present in 94 patients. In 575 patients, at least three different autoimmune phenomena were present. We concluded that thyroid autoimmunity and antibodies suggestive for celiac disease are the most prevalent additional immune phenomena in type 1 diabetes. Parietal/adrenal antibodies are rare.
passage_3: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.

Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

question: What were the main findings of the Practical Aspects and Exercise Safety Benefits of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in Type 1 Diabetes.txt study?
passage_1: Practical Aspects and Exercise Safety Benefits of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in Type 1 Diabetes evaluates the effectiveness, operational mechanisms, and practical management strategies of automated insulin delivery (AID) systems during and after exercise in individuals with type 1 diabetes. The authors find that while AID technology modestly improves time in range and reduces hypoglycemia during physical activity, inherent limitations in the pharmacodynamics of subcutaneously administered rapid-acting insulins prevent systems from fully adjusting to sudden exercise-induced glycemic shifts or rapid changes in insulin requirements. To optimize safety and glycemic control, the paper recommends setting elevated glucose targets (typically 140–160 mg/dL or system-specific exercise/activity modes) starting 1–2 hours prior to planned exercise lasting 30 minutes or longer, and extending these targets into post-exercise recovery or overnight when necessary to prevent delayed hypoglycemia. Additionally, guidelines suggest reducing mealtime bolus doses by 25–75% for exercise occurring within 1–3 hours after meals, using perceived exertion scales (like the modified Borg scale) to differentiate aerobic activities requiring higher targets from anaerobic exercises that may trigger temporary glycemic spikes, and utilizing carbohydrate supplementation or temporary pump suspensions during unplanned or spontaneous physical activity.
passage_2: The study Time in Range for Closed-Loop Systems versus Standard of Care during Physical Exercise in People with Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis evaluates the comparison of time in range (70–180 mg/dL or 3.9–10.0 mmol/L) between fully closed-loop systems and standard of care during physical exercise in people with type 1 diabetes across six randomized controlled trials involving 153 participants (analyzed as 266 participants across 12 comparisons due to crossover designs). The findings reveal that closed-loop systems moderately improved overall time in range during exercise compared to standard of care with an absolute mean difference of 6.18%, with a particularly pronounced and significant benefit in children and adolescents (absolute mean difference of 9.46%) compared to adults (absolute mean difference of 1.07%). Additionally, physical exercise performed on a cycle ergometer demonstrated beneficial effects of closed-loop systems on time in range (mean difference of 12.34%), whereas treadmill exercise and skiing sessions did not show a statistically significant difference. The authors note recommendations highlighting the importance of physical activity for health benefits and mention position statement guidelines concerning glycemic management around exercise—pointing out that continuous glucose monitor accuracy can deteriorate during acute exercise due to physiological lag time between interstitial and blood glucose—and conclude that while closed-loop systems effectively support glycemic control during exercise, further advancement in sensor technology and algorithms is needed to manage rapid glucose fluctuations.
passage_3: The Type 1 Diabetes Exercise Initiative Pediatric (T1DEXIP) Study evaluates 24-hour postexercise glycemia and overnight hypoglycemia risk in adolescents with type 1 diabetes in a real-world setting, analyzing data from 251 participants across 3,319 exercise sessions. The study found that maximal glucose drops occurred 8 to 16 hours after exercise, with larger drops during activity being associated with lower mean glucose levels immediately post-exercise and 12 to 16 hours later; overall, nocturnal hypoglycemia occurred on 14% of post-exercise nights (compared to 12% on sedentary days), with significantly higher rates when average total daily activity was at least 60 minutes, during longer individual exercise sessions, in youth with longer diabetes duration or lower HbA1c, with conventional pump use, and when time below range was at least 4% in the preceding 24 hours. While explicit clinical guidelines were not provided in the paper, the authors highlight that regular physical activity should be prescribed and encouraged for youth with type 1 diabetes (matching the general pediatric recommendation of 60 minutes daily) and recommend leveraging these participant- and event-level findings to inform new clinical guidelines, decision support tools, and refined automated closed-loop insulin delivery algorithms to better mitigate exercise-related hypoglycemia.

To optimize safety and glycemic control, the paper recommends setting elevated glucose targets (typically 140–160 mg/dL or system-specific exercise/activity modes) starting 1–2 hours prior to planned exercise lasting 30 minutes or longer, and extending these targets into post-exercise recovery or overnight when necessary to prevent delayed hypoglycemia. Additionally, guidelines suggest reducing mealtime bolus doses by 25–75% for exercise occurring within 1–3 hours after meals, using perceived exertion scales (like the modified Borg scale) to differentiate aerobic activities requiring higher targets from anaerobic exercises that may trigger temporary glycemic spikes, and utilizing carbohydrate supplementation or temporary pump suspensions during unplanned or spontaneous physical activity.
