question: What population was studied in the Predictivity of Thyroid Autoantibodies for the Development of Thyroid Disorders in Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes.txt cross-sectional study?
passage_1: "Predictivity of thyroid autoantibodies for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes" investigates the prevalence of thyroid autoantibodies and their significance for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes. Antibodies to thyroglobulin (anti-TG) and thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) were measured in 216 patients (113 boys; median age 12.9 years (range 1-22 years)) with Type 1 diabetes (diabetes duration 2.5 years (0-14 years)) in a cross-sectional study. Sixteen patients with significantly elevated anti-TPO titres were followed longitudinally (6.0 years (4-13 years)) including the measurement of anti-TPO, anti-TG, T(3), T(4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ultrasound assessment. Twenty-two patients (10.0%) had significantly elevated titres of anti-TPO, 19 (8.7%) of anti-TG and 13 (5.9%) of both autoantibodies. Girls had more frequently elevated anti-TPO antibodies than boys (P < 0.05). Eight of 16 patients (50%) developed thyroid disorders defined by a TSH elevation (> or = 4.5 microU/ml) and/or sonographic thyroid abnormalities during a median time of 3.5 years (2-6 years) after first detection of anti-TPO positivity. They were characterized by higher levels of anti-TPO (P = 0.001) and a more frequent coexistence of anti-TG antibodies (P = 0.002) than those with no development of thyroid disorder even after an observation period of 5.5 years (5-10 years). We concluded that because 50% of children with diabetes and significant titres of anti-TPO develop thyroid problems within 3-4 years, examinations of thyroid antibodies should be performed yearly. In cases of significant antibody titres, thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment are recommended in order to minimize the risk of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in these patients.
passage_2: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.
passage_3: "Younger age at onset and sex predict celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: an Italian multicenter study" estimates the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in Italian children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and to assess whether age at onset of type 1 diabetes is independently associated with diagnosis of celiac disease. The study group was a clinic-based cohort of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes cared for in 25 Italian centers for childhood diabetes. Yearly screening for celiac disease was performed using IgA/IgG anti-gliadin and IgA anti-endomysium antibodies. Of the 4,322 children and adolescents (age 11.8 ± 4.2 years) identified with type 1 diabetes, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was diagnosed in 292 (prevalence 6.8%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–7.6), with a higher risk seen in girls than in boys (odds ratio [OR] 1.93, 1.51–2.47). In 89% of these, diabetes was diagnosed before celiac disease. In logistic regression analyses, being younger at onset of diabetes, being female, and having a diagnosis of a thyroid disorder were independently associated with the risk of having diabetes and celiac disease. In comparison with subjects who were older than 9 years at onset of diabetes, subjects who were younger than 4 years at onset had an OR of 3.27 (2.20–4.85). We have provided evidence that 1) the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes is high (6.8%); 2) the risk of having both diseases is threefold higher in children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age <4 years than in those age >9 years; and 3) girls have a higher risk of having both diseases than boys.

passage_1: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

Sixteen patients with significantly elevated anti-TPO titres were followed longitudinally (6.0 years (4-13 years)) including the measurement of anti-TPO, anti-TG, T(3), T(4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ultrasound assessment. Twenty-two patients (10.0%) had significantly elevated titres of anti-TPO, 19 (8.7%) of anti-TG and 13 (5.9%) of both autoantibodies. Girls had more frequently elevated anti-TPO antibodies than boys (P < 0.05). Eight of 16 patients (50%) developed thyroid disorders defined by a TSH elevation (> or = 4.5 microU/ml) and/or sonographic thyroid abnormalities during a median time of 3.5 years (2-6 years) after first detection of anti-TPO positivity. They were characterized by higher levels of anti-TPO (P = 0.001) and a more frequent coexistence of anti-TG antibodies (P = 0.002) than those with no development of thyroid disorder even after an observation period of 5.5 years (5-10 years). We concluded that because 50% of children with diabetes and significant titres of anti-TPO develop thyroid problems within 3-4 years, examinations of thyroid antibodies should be performed yearly. In cases of significant antibody titres, thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment are recommended in order to minimize the risk of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in these patients.

As currently no data are available on the prevalence of SCH and its potential association with lipoprotein profile in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1DM), we investigated the prevalence of SCH and associated lipid levels in young diabetic patients. Cross-sectional analysis of 22,747 children, adolescents, and young adults (age <25 years) with T1DM with normal T3 and T4 and either normal TSH (≥0.5 to <4.0 mIU/l, euthyroid group) or elevated TSH (≥4.0 to <25.0 mIU/l, SCH group) and simultaneous measurement of serum lipid and lipoprotein status. The prevalence rate of SCH in the study population was 7.2%. Adjusted for age, gender, diabetes duration, current insulin dose, HbA1c, and BMI z-score, patients with SCH had significantly higher levels of total cholesterol (178.7 vs 175.3 mg/dl, P<0.001) and LDL-cholesterol (97.0 vs 93.7 mg/dl, P<0.001) compared with euthyroid patients. SCH-associated increases in lipid and lipoprotein levels may therefore add to an increased long-term cardiovascular risk in young patients with T1DM.

question: What were the main findings of the Pregnancy Outcomes in Young Women With Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Followed in the TODAY Study.txt study?
passage_1: "Pregnancy Outcomes in Young Women With Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Followed in the TODAY Study" evaluates maternal and fetal outcomes among 141 young women with youth-onset type 2 diabetes who experienced a total of 260 pregnancies over a maximum follow-up of 15 years. The study found high rates of maternal and neonatal complications: 65% of women experienced pregnancy complications, 35% had chronic hypertension, 25% had pre-pregnancy nephropathy, and 31.9% maintained elevated HbA1c levels (≥8%). Regarding outcomes, pregnancy loss occurred in 25.3% of cases and preterm birth in 32.6%, while offspring showed rates of 7.8% small for gestational age, 26.8% large for gestational age, and 17.9% macrosomia. Notably, prior contraception use was reported by only 13.5% of the participants. The authors conclude that these substantial maternal and infant risks—exacerbated by significant socioeconomic disadvantage—could potentially be mitigated through higher rates of contraception use and improved reproductive planning in this population.
passage_2: “Retinopathy in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes Participating in the TODAY Clinical Trial” evaluates the prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in a cohort of 517 youth (aged 10–17 years at baseline) with type 2 diabetes of 2 to 8 years duration using standardized central grading of fundus photographs. The study found an overall retinopathy prevalence of 13.7%, with all affected participants exhibiting mild or very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and no cases of macular edema or proliferative disease. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. Although specific clinical recommendations and guidelines were not provided, the authors note that the natural history and progression of diabetic retinopathy in youth with type 2 diabetes will be further clarified through continued follow-up of this cohort.
passage_3: The “Characteristics of adolescents and youth with recent-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY cohort at baseline” evaluates the baseline demographic, clinical, medical history, and biochemical characteristics of 704 American adolescents and youth aged 10 to 17 years who were diagnosed with recent-onset type 2 diabetes for less than two years and had a body mass index at or above the 85th percentile. The findings reveal that the participant group was predominantly female (64.9%), had a mean age of 14.0 years, and consisted mostly of racial and ethnic minority populations, including 41.1% Hispanic and 31.5% non-Hispanic Black youth, with 89.4% having a family history of diabetes and significant socioeconomic challenges such as 41.5% residing in households earning less than $25,000 annually. Furthermore, clinical and biochemical comorbidities were highly prevalent within two years of diagnosis, including low high-density lipoprotein levels in 79.8%, blood pressure at or above the 90th percentile in 26.3%, microalbuminuria in 13.0%, and elevated triglycerides in 10.2% of participants. The study does not explicitly provide formal clinical practice guidelines or recommendations, but it emphasizes that youth-onset type 2 diabetes presents with substantial risk factors and metabolic abnormalities early in the course of the disease.

question: What were the main findings of the Prevalence and Correlates of Depressed Mood Among Youth With Diabetes The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study.txt study?
passage_1: "Prevalence and Correlates of Depressed Mood Among Youth With Diabetes: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study" evaluates whether depressed mood among youth with diabetes is associated with diabetes type, duration, mean glycosylated hemoglobin HbA1c level, and the frequency of diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycemic episodes, hospitalizations, and emergency department visits. In a sample of 2,672 youth aged 10 to 21 years with a mean diabetes duration of 5 years, 14% exhibited mildly depressed mood (CES-D 16–23) and 8.6% exhibited moderately or severely depressed mood (CES-D ≥ 24), with overall prevalence rates comparable to published estimates for youth without diabetes. Females reported higher mean depression scores than males, and after adjusting for demographic factors and diabetes duration, depressed mood was found to be higher among males with type 2 diabetes than those with type 1 diabetes, as well as higher among females with comorbidities than those without. Higher mean HbA1c levels and higher frequency of emergency department visits were significantly associated with depressed mood, prompting the recommendation that physicians and healthcare professionals consider screening youth with diabetes for depressed mood in clinical settings, especially targeting youth with poor glycemic control, frequent emergency department visits, males with type 2 diabetes, and females with comorbidities.
passage_2: The study "Mental health comorbidity and youth onset type 2 diabetes: A systematic review of the literature" evaluates the current literature surrounding youth with depression and type 2 diabetes (T2D), specifically reviewing 13 publications from 8 studies involving 2,244 individuals aged 6 to 17. The findings indicate that while depressive symptoms are common in youth with T2D and correlate with negative T2D outcomes, most studies failed to formally assess for major depressive disorder (MDD) and actively excluded participants with a prior MDD diagnosis. Based on these gaps, the authors recommend that future research focus on four key areas: including youth with diagnosed MDD, conducting treatment studies addressing both T2D and MDD concurrently, analyzing larger and more racially diverse youth samples, and evaluating how social determinants of health alongside mental health comorbidities impact T2D outcomes.
passage_3: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.

The study found a DPN prevalence of 7% in youth with type 1 diabetes and 22% in youth with type 2 diabetes. For participants with type 1 diabetes, risk factors associated with DPN included older age, longer diabetes duration, smoking, elevated diastolic blood pressure, obesity, increased LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, lower HDL cholesterol, and poorer long-term glycemic control over time. In youth with type 2 diabetes, DPN was associated with older age, male sex, longer diabetes duration, smoking, and lower HDL cholesterol, with youth with type 2 diabetes having nearly three times higher odds of DPN compared to those with type 1 diabetes even after adjusting for key covariates. The study found that after adjusting for completeness of ascertainment, the overall prevalence of type 1 diabetes increased by 21.1% across all demographic subgroups except American Indians and children aged 0 to 4 years, while the overall prevalence of type 2 diabetes among adolescents aged 10 to 19 years increased by 30.5%, with significant rises observed among white, black, and Hispanic youth. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. The findings indicate that while behavioral interventions utilizing CBT principles have a superior positive impact on regimen adherence, metabolic control improves significantly through CST and certain CBT approaches, and stress management and psychotherapy show strong promise in helping adolescents manage daily diabetes-related stressors. Consequently, the review suggests that psychological interventions hold promise for enhancing diabetes management in youth, though additional research is required to better understand their specific effects.

question: What were the main findings of the Psychometric Properties of the Parent and Child Problem Areas in Diabetes Measures.txt study?
passage_1: The study on the psychometric properties of the Parent and Child Problem Areas in Diabetes Measures evaluates the reliability and validity of adapted survey instruments (PAID-C for youth ages 8–12 and P-PAID-C for their parents) to measure diabetes-specific emotional distress across a sample of 804 children with type 1 diabetes and 968 parents recruited from 42 U.S. diabetes camps. Factor analyses supported an 11-item, two-factor structure for the child measure (capturing emotional burden and regimen-specific distress) and a 16-item, four-factor second-order structure for the parent measure (capturing negative emotions, keeping up with chronic demands, personal regimen-specific distress, and child regimen-specific distress), with both tools demonstrating high internal consistency and criterion validity through positive correlations with HbA1c and negative correlations with diabetes-related strengths and self-care skills. The authors recommend utilizing these brief, standardized measures for routine, clinic-based screening to enable early identification of diabetes-specific emotional distress, guide clinical decision-making, and inform timely interventions before distress negatively impacts glycemic outcomes or leads to diabetes burnout.
passage_2: Psychometric Properties of the Parent and Child Problem Areas in Diabetes Measures evaluates the validity and reliability of adapted child (PAID-C) and parent (P-PAID-C) versions of the Problem Areas in Diabetes Scale designed to assess diabetes-specific emotional distress in children ages 8–12 with type 1 diabetes and their caregivers across 42 summer camps in the United States. The study found that the 11-item, two-factor child measure (covering emotional burden and regimen-specific distress; Cronbach’s α = 0.91) and the 16-item parent measure (structured around four factors: negative emotions, keeping up with chronic demands, personal regimen-specific distress, and child regimen-specific distress; Cronbach’s α = 0.92) both demonstrated strong internal consistency and construct validity. Higher distress scores on both versions significantly correlated with higher HbA1c levels, lower diabetes-related strengths, and lower parent-reported self-care skills, supporting criterion validity. Based on these findings, the paper recommends incorporating routine, clinic-based screening using the PAID-C and P-PAID-C to identify diabetes distress early, facilitate targeted interventions, and guide clinical decision-making to prevent diabetes burnout and regimen mismanagement.
passage_3: "Disordered Eating Behaviors and Eating Disorders in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review" evaluates disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) in youth diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by identifying the most common DEBs, analyzing potential risk and protective factors, and reviewing existing screening tools and interventions utilized for this population. Findings indicate that approximately half of the youth study participants had elevated scores on the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised, showing a higher likelihood of engaging in DEBs compared to youth with type 1 diabetes, with key risk factors including obesity, body weight/shape concerns, and caregiver subclinical binge eating. Recommendations highlight a critical need for further research to construct a framework for understanding influential variables, to advance screening tools, and to design effective targeted interventions.

passage_1: "Transfer from pediatric to adult health care: effects on diabetes outcomes" evaluates the impact of transitioning from pediatric to adult diabetes care on emerging adults with type 1 diabetes, focusing on outcomes such as diabetes care visit attendance, glycemic control, and acute diabetes-related complications while assessing the methodological strength of existing observational and interventional studies. The paper's findings indicate that while observational studies often report a decline in diabetes care visit frequency alongside an improvement or no change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) after transfer, these results are heavily limited by methodological flaws, including incomplete data, high dropout rates among patients who drop out of follow-up, lack of appropriate comparison groups, and confounding physical and psychosocial maturation. Furthermore, studies tracking patients who left the pediatric health system for a broad array of adult providers found deterioration in glycemic control compared to peers remaining in pediatric care, and structured transition interventions showed temporary benefits in clinic attendance or HbA1c that were often not sustained long-term. Regarding recommendations and guidelines, the paper does not propose new clinical guidelines or structured transition protocols; instead, it highlights a critical lack of methodologically strong empirical evidence—noting that most current recommendations are based on expert consensus or clinical experience—and emphasizes that future research must address these shortcomings by utilizing proper comparison groups, tracking patients across diverse adult care settings, and accounting for patient attrition to properly guide clinicians and improve emerging adult care.
passage_2: The study Obesity in youth with type 1 diabetes in Germany, Austria, and the United States examined the prevalence of obesity among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) using data from two large pediatric clinical registries in the United States and Europe—the T1D Exchange (n = 11,435) and the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (n = 21,501). Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Furthermore, higher BMI z-scores were significantly associated with elevated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and a higher frequency of severe hypoglycemia across both groups, suggesting that obesity presents additional challenges to achieving optimal glycemic control in young individuals with type 1 diabetes.

The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

question: What were the main findings of the Real Time Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Can Improve Quality of Life.txt rct?
passage_1: "Real-time continuous glucose monitoring in adolescents and young adults with type 2 diabetes can improve quality of life" reported that real-time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is effective for diabetes management in cases of type 1 diabetes and adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) but has not been assessed in adolescents and young adults (AYAs) with T2D. The objective of this pilot interventional study was to assess the feasibility and acceptability of real-time CGM use in AYAs with T2D. Adolescents and young adults (13-21 years old) with T2D for six months or more and hemoglobin A1c (A1c) greater than 7%, on any Food and Drug Administration-approved treatment regimen, were included. After a blinded run-in period, participants were given access to a real-time CGM system for 12 weeks. The use and acceptability of the real-time CGM were evaluated by sensor usage, surveys, and focus group qualitative data. Participants' (n = 9) median age was 19.1 (interquartile range [IQR] 16.8-20.5) years, 78% were female, 100% were people of color, and 67% were publicly insured. Baseline A1c was 11.9% (standard deviation ±2.8%), with median diabetes duration of 2.5 (IQR 1.4-6) years, and 67% were using insulin. Seven participants completed the study and demonstrated statistically significant improvement in diabetes-related quality of life, with the mean Pediatric Quality of Life inventory (PedsQL) diabetes score increasing from 70 to 75 after using CGM (P = .026). Focus group results supported survey results that CGM use among AYAs with T2D is feasible, can improve quality of life, and has the potential to modify behavior. We concluded that real-time CGM is feasible and acceptable for AYAs with T2D and may improve the quality of life of patients with diabetes. Larger randomized controlled trials are needed to assess the effects on glycemic control and healthy lifestyle changes.

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.

question: What conclusions did the Rethinking funding priorities in mental health research.txt authors draw?
passage_1: "Rethinking funding priorities in mental health research" evaluates the distribution of research investments in high-income countries—particularly at the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)—arguing that a heavy skew toward long-term, neurobiological mechanism research comes at the expense of shorter-term prevention and treatment strategies. The paper finds that basic and translational neuroscience accounts for approximately 85% of the NIMH non-HIV/AIDS budget, leaving only around 15% for services and interventions research, despite substantial immediate public health needs and high rates of unmet mental health care. The authors recommend a rebalancing and diversification of the mental health research portfolio to allocate greater funding toward scalable, cost-efficient interventions, implementation science, suicide prevention, and addressing social determinants of health. Finally, they provide guidelines calling for broad, international stakeholder participation across public, legislative, and scientific forums to re-evaluate funding allocations, evaluate implementation evidence in routine practice settings, and ensure immediate public health impacts alongside the long-term search for neurobiological cures.
passage_2: The clinical report Promoting Optimal Development: Screening for Mental Health, Emotional, and Behavioral Problems evaluates the increasing prevalence of mental health, emotional, and behavioral (MEB) issues among children and outlines updated guidance for pediatric primary care clinicians to effectively screen, identify, and manage these conditions. The report notes that 13% to 20% of U.S. children have a diagnosed MEB disorder—with ADHD, anxiety, disruptive behavior, and mood disorders being the most common—and highlights rising suicide rates alongside exacerbated post-pandemic mental health distress. To address significant gaps in detection and a severe shortage of subspecialist clinicians, the guidelines recommend starting caregiver-focused screening within the first month of life for postpartum depression, followed by child-focused MEB screening at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months, alternating with developmental and autism screenings, and continuing annually after age 3. Additionally, the clinical report provides recommendations on using standardized, culturally responsive screening tools, managing positive screens within the pediatric medical home, promoting family resilience, and overcoming practice-level barriers to streamline workflow and improve care integration.
passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

question: What were the main findings of the Risk of diabetic retinopathy at first screen in children at 12 and 13 years of age.txt study?
passage_1: The study “Risk of diabetic retinopathy at first screen in children at 12 and 13 years of age” evaluates the relationships between age at diagnosis of diabetes, age at diabetic eye screening, and the severity of diabetic retinopathy at the first and subsequent screenings in children aged 12 or 13 years. Analyzing data from 2,125 children across screening programs in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the findings reveal that children diagnosed with diabetes at age 2 or younger had a 20% and 11% proportion of retinopathy at age 12 and 13 respectively, which decreased to 8% and 2% for those diagnosed between ages 2 and 12, with only three children aged 8, 10, and 11 years at diagnosis having images graded with referable retinopathy. Over a mean follow-up of 3.1 years, referable retinopathy developed at a low incidence rate of 4.7 per 1,000 person-years. Based on these findings, the authors conclude with the recommendation that diabetic retinopathy screening earlier than age 12 is not necessary.
passage_2: The study “Screening eye exams in youth with type 1 diabetes under 18 years of age: once may be enough?” evaluates the optimal frequency and necessity of eye screening examinations in pediatric patients under 18 years of age with type 1 diabetes, drawing on long-term data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) research group. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

question: What were the main findings of the Safety and Tolerability of the Treatment of Youth Onset Type 2 Diabetes The TODAY Experience.txt clinical trial?
passage_1: "Efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in children and young adults with type 2 diabetes: a prospective, multicentre, randomised, parallel group, phase 3 study" reported that since there are few treatment options for young people with type 2 diabetes, we aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin as add-on therapy in children, adolescents, and young adults with type 2 diabetes receiving metformin, insulin, or both. This multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised phase 3 study was undertaken at 30 centres in five countries (Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Russia, and the USA). Participants aged 10-24 years with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c concentration of 6·5-11% (48-97 mmol/mol) were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo during a 24 week double-blind period, which was then followed by a 28 week open-label safety extension in which all participants received dapagliflozin. Participants and study personnel were masked and participants were randomly assigned treatment (placebo or study drug) using an interactive web and voice response system. The primary outcome was between-group differences in change in HbA1c concentration from baseline to 24 weeks (intention-to-treat analysis). A prespecified sensitivity analysis of the primary outcome was also assessed in the per-protocol population, which included only protocol-compliant participants. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02725593. Between June 22, 2016, and March 15, 2019, 72 participants (19 [26%] of whom were aged 18-24 years) were randomly assigned (39 to dapagliflozin and 33 to placebo). Mean age was 16·1 (SD 3·3) years. In the intention-to-treat analysis, after 24 weeks, mean change in HbA1c concentration was -0·25% (95% CI -0·85 to 0·34; -2·7 [-9·3 to 3·7] mmol/mol) for dapagliflozin and 0·50% (-0·18 to 1·17; 5·5 [-2·0 to 12·8] mmol/mol) for placebo. The between-group difference was -0·75% (95% CI -1·65 to 0·15; -8·2 [-18·0 to 1·6] mmol/mol; p=0·10).
passage_2: "Safety and tolerability of the treatment of youth-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY experience" reported that data related to the safety and tolerability of treatments for pediatric type 2 diabetes are limited. The TODAY clinical trial assessed severe adverse events (SAEs) and targeted nonsevere adverse events (AEs) before and after treatment failure, which was the primary outcome (PO). Obese 10- to 17-year-olds (N = 699) with type 2 diabetes for <2 years and hemoglobin A1c (A1C) ≤ 8% on metformin monotherapy were randomized to one of three treatments: metformin, metformin plus rosiglitazone (M + R), or metformin plus lifestyle program (M + L). Participants were followed for 2-6.5 years. Gastrointestinal (GI) disturbance was the most common AE (41%) and was lower in the M + R group (P = 0.018). Other common AEs included anemia (20% before PO, 14% after PO), abnormal liver transaminases (16, 15%), excessive weight gain (7, 9%), and psychological events (10, 18%); the AEs were similar across treatments. Permanent medication reductions/discontinuations occurred most often because of abnormal liver transaminases and were lowest in the M + R group (P = 0.005). Treatment-emergent SAEs were uncommon and similar across treatments. Most (98%) were unrelated or unlikely related to the study intervention. There were no deaths and only 18 targeted SAEs (diabetic ketoacidosis, n = 12; severe hypoglycemia, n = 5; lactic acidosis, n = 1). There were 62 pregnancies occurring in 45 participants, and 6 infants had congenital anomalies. We concluded that the TODAY study represents extensive experience managing type 2 diabetes in youth and found that the three treatment approaches were generally safe and well tolerated. Adding rosiglitazone to metformin may reduce GI side effects and hepatotoxicity.
passage_3: The “Safety and Tolerability of the Treatment of Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes: The TODAY experience” evaluates the safety, tolerability, and event rates of three distinct treatment strategies—metformin monotherapy, metformin plus rosiglitazone, and metformin plus an intensive lifestyle intervention—in 699 obese adolescents aged 10–17 with youth-onset type 2 diabetes followed over 2 to 6.5 years. The study found that all three treatment approaches were generally safe and well tolerated, with low rates of treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) and no reported deaths. Gastrointestinal disturbance was the most common nonsevere adverse event (41%), though it occurred less frequently in the metformin plus rosiglitazone group, which also experienced significantly lower rates of study medication dose reductions or discontinuations due to elevated liver transaminases. Targeted serious adverse events were rare across all groups and included 12 cases of diabetic ketoacidosis, 5 of severe hypoglycemia, and 1 of lactic acidosis associated with severe asthma, alongside 62 pregnancies yielding 6 congenital anomalies. Based on these findings, the paper concludes that combining rosiglitazone with metformin may reduce gastrointestinal side effects and hepatotoxicity in youth with type 2 diabetes.

question: What were the long-term outcomes beyond the study period in the Safety and Tolerability of the Treatment of Youth Onset Type 2 Diabetes The TODAY Experience.txt clinical trial?
passage_1: The "TODAY Reflects on the Changing Faces of Type 2 Diabetes" study evaluates the efficacy, safety, and longitudinal outcomes of three treatment strategies—metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, and metformin plus intensive lifestyle changes—in maintaining glycemic control among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The paper highlights findings demonstrating that metformin monotherapy achieved durable glycemic control in only about half of the youth, whereas the combination of metformin and rosiglitazone significantly improved glycemic durability due to favorable effects on insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function. Although the treatment approaches were generally safe with primarily gastrointestinal side effects, the study interventions were inadequate to prevent the progression of cardiovascular and renal risk factors, as dyslipidemia, chronic inflammation, hypertension, and microalbuminuria worsened over time regardless of diabetes treatment. Considering projections of up to a fourfold increase in youth type 2 diabetes, the commentary emphasizes the critical recommendation for immediate research, screening, medical interventions, and public policy changes to slow and reverse the growing health and economic burden of adolescent-onset type 2 diabetes.
passage_2: "A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes (TODAY)” study evaluates the efficacy of three treatment regimens—metformin alone, metformin combined with rosiglitazone, and metformin combined with an intensive lifestyle-intervention program—in achieving durable glycemic control among children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that metformin plus rosiglitazone was particularly effective in girls, while metformin monotherapy was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants. Serious adverse events occurred in 19.2% of participants across the trial, and although the paper does not explicitly state formal clinical recommendations or guidelines, it concludes that metformin monotherapy fails to maintain durable glycemic control in roughly half of youth with type 2 diabetes and that adding rosiglitazone provides superior glycemic durability compared to monotherapy or intensive lifestyle interventions.
passage_3: "Safety and tolerability of the treatment of youth-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY experience" reported that data related to the safety and tolerability of treatments for pediatric type 2 diabetes are limited. The TODAY clinical trial assessed severe adverse events (SAEs) and targeted nonsevere adverse events (AEs) before and after treatment failure, which was the primary outcome (PO). Obese 10- to 17-year-olds (N = 699) with type 2 diabetes for <2 years and hemoglobin A1c (A1C) ≤ 8% on metformin monotherapy were randomized to one of three treatments: metformin, metformin plus rosiglitazone (M + R), or metformin plus lifestyle program (M + L). Participants were followed for 2-6.5 years. Gastrointestinal (GI) disturbance was the most common AE (41%) and was lower in the M + R group (P = 0.018). Other common AEs included anemia (20% before PO, 14% after PO), abnormal liver transaminases (16, 15%), excessive weight gain (7, 9%), and psychological events (10, 18%); the AEs were similar across treatments. Permanent medication reductions/discontinuations occurred most often because of abnormal liver transaminases and were lowest in the M + R group (P = 0.005). Treatment-emergent SAEs were uncommon and similar across treatments. Most (98%) were unrelated or unlikely related to the study intervention. There were no deaths and only 18 targeted SAEs (diabetic ketoacidosis, n = 12; severe hypoglycemia, n = 5; lactic acidosis, n = 1). There were 62 pregnancies occurring in 45 participants, and 6 infants had congenital anomalies. We concluded that the TODAY study represents extensive experience managing type 2 diabetes in youth and found that the three treatment approaches were generally safe and well tolerated. Adding rosiglitazone to metformin may reduce GI side effects and hepatotoxicity.

question: What were the main findings of the Safety and Tolerability of the Treatment of Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes The TODAY experience.txt study?
passage_1: "Efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in children and young adults with type 2 diabetes: a prospective, multicentre, randomised, parallel group, phase 3 study" reported that since there are few treatment options for young people with type 2 diabetes, we aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin as add-on therapy in children, adolescents, and young adults with type 2 diabetes receiving metformin, insulin, or both. This multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised phase 3 study was undertaken at 30 centres in five countries (Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Russia, and the USA). Participants aged 10-24 years with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c concentration of 6·5-11% (48-97 mmol/mol) were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo during a 24 week double-blind period, which was then followed by a 28 week open-label safety extension in which all participants received dapagliflozin. Participants and study personnel were masked and participants were randomly assigned treatment (placebo or study drug) using an interactive web and voice response system. The primary outcome was between-group differences in change in HbA1c concentration from baseline to 24 weeks (intention-to-treat analysis). A prespecified sensitivity analysis of the primary outcome was also assessed in the per-protocol population, which included only protocol-compliant participants. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02725593. Between June 22, 2016, and March 15, 2019, 72 participants (19 [26%] of whom were aged 18-24 years) were randomly assigned (39 to dapagliflozin and 33 to placebo). Mean age was 16·1 (SD 3·3) years. In the intention-to-treat analysis, after 24 weeks, mean change in HbA1c concentration was -0·25% (95% CI -0·85 to 0·34; -2·7 [-9·3 to 3·7] mmol/mol) for dapagliflozin and 0·50% (-0·18 to 1·17; 5·5 [-2·0 to 12·8] mmol/mol) for placebo. The between-group difference was -0·75% (95% CI -1·65 to 0·15; -8·2 [-18·0 to 1·6] mmol/mol; p=0·10).

Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.

Findings indicate that approximately half of the youth study participants had elevated scores on the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised, showing a higher likelihood of engaging in DEBs compared to youth with type 1 diabetes, with key risk factors including obesity, body weight/shape concerns, and caregiver subclinical binge eating. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.

Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. question: What were the main findings of the Screening for Celiac Disease in Type 1 Diabetes A Systematic Review.txt systematic review?
passage_1: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.
passage_2: "Associated auto-immune disease in type 1 diabetes patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis" reported that the association between type 1 diabetes (T1D) and other auto-immune diseases is well known. However, a quantitative overview of all associated auto-immune diseases and their prevalence in T1D is lacking. Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE and Cochrane library in September 2018 to identify relevant articles about the prevalence of the following associated auto-immune diseases in T1D cohorts: auto-immune thyroid disease, celiac disease, gastric autoimmunity including pernicious anemia, vitiligo and adrenal gland insufficiency. A meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled prevalence using a random-effects model. Furthermore, random-effects meta-regression analysis was performed to assess the association between prevalence and mean age or diabetes duration. Results One hundred eighty articles were eligible including a total of 293 889 type 1 diabetes patients. Hypothyroidism (65 studies) was prevalent in 9.8% (95% CI: 7.5-12.3) of patients. Meta-regression showed that for every 10-year age increase, hypothyroidism prevalence increased 4.6% (95% CI: 2.6-6.6, P < 0.000, 54 studies). Weighted prevalence of celiac disease was 4.5% (95% CI: 4.0-5.5, 87 studies). Gastric autoimmunity was found in 4.3% of patients (95% CI: 1.6-8.2, 8 studies) and vitiligo in 2.4% (95% CI: 1.2-3.9, 14 studies) of patients. The prevalence of adrenal insufficiency was 0.2% (95% CI: 0.0-0.4, 14 studies) and hyperthyroidism was found in 1.3 percent (95% CI: 0.9-1.8, 45 studies) of type 1 diabetes patients. For all analyses, statistical heterogeneity between studies was moderate to high. Conclusions The prevalence of antibody-mediated auto-immune disease is high among type 1 diabetes patients. Especially hypothyroidism and celiac disease are frequently found.

Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.
passage_2: The study Obesity in youth with type 1 diabetes in Germany, Austria, and the United States examined the prevalence of obesity among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) using data from two large pediatric clinical registries in the United States and Europe—the T1D Exchange (n = 11,435) and the Diabetes Prospective Follow-up (n = 21,501). Comparing participants aged 2 to under 18 years against national and international body mass index (BMI) references, researchers found that median BMI values in both registries exceeded standard reference values, indicating that excessive weight is a widespread issue among children with T1D, particularly in the U.S. While no significant BMI differences were found among children aged 2–5 years across the registries, US participants in older age groups (6–17 years) exhibited significantly higher BMI z-scores (P < 0.001). Furthermore, higher BMI z-scores were significantly associated with elevated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and a higher frequency of severe hypoglycemia across both groups, suggesting that obesity presents additional challenges to achieving optimal glycemic control in young individuals with type 1 diabetes.

Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). question: What were the main findings of the Sex and Age Dependent Effects of Celiac Disease on Growth and Weight Gain in Children With Type 1 Diabetes Analysis of the Type 1 Diabetes Exchange Clinic Registry.txt study?
passage_1: "Sex- and age-dependent effects of celiac disease on growth and weight gain in children with type 1 diabetes: analysis of the Type 1 Diabetes Exchange Clinic Registry" reports that celiac disease (CD) is common in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and effects of CD on growth in children with T1D remain unclear. We analyzed heights, weights, and body mass index (BMI) in 215 matched pediatric CD/control pairs in the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry. CD was defined by a clinic-reported diagnosis and positive celiac serology (n = 80) and/or positive small bowel biopsy (n = 135). Cases and controls were matched by age (mean: 14 years), diabetes duration (median: 7 years), sex (57% female), and clinic site. There were 5569 height/weight measurements. Gluten was restricted for varying periods of time in 61% of females and 51% of males with CD. Females with CD were shorter than female controls at all ages (P = 0.01). Weight z-scores were initially lower in preschool females with CD but similar to controls by middle childhood. Males with CD were initially shorter but adult heights were similar. Height in both sexes and weight in males were lower in CD participants diagnosed at younger age. Growth in T1D children with biopsy-proven CD, 76% of them were gluten-restricted, was comparable to that of T1D controls. We concluded that concurrent CD impairs linear growth in T1D females at all stages of development and in young T1D males. Young females with CD have lower weights, but both sexes have similar weights by middle childhood. Children younger at CD onset remain shorter throughout childhood; males younger at CD onset have persistently lower weights. Long-term gluten restriction may restore weight gain and linear growth in children with CD and T1D.

The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). question: What were the main findings of the Subclinical Hypothyroidism and Dyslipidemia in Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.txt study?
passage_1: "Subclinical hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reports that recent epidemiological evidence suggests that subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH), defined as elevated TSH concentrations with normal circulating levels of triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4), is associated with dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disease in adult populations. As currently no data are available on the prevalence of SCH and its potential association with lipoprotein profile in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1DM), we investigated the prevalence of SCH and associated lipid levels in young diabetic patients. Cross-sectional analysis of 22,747 children, adolescents, and young adults (age <25 years) with T1DM with normal T3 and T4 and either normal TSH (≥0.5 to <4.0 mIU/l, euthyroid group) or elevated TSH (≥4.0 to <25.0 mIU/l, SCH group) and simultaneous measurement of serum lipid and lipoprotein status. The prevalence rate of SCH in the study population was 7.2%. Adjusted for age, gender, diabetes duration, current insulin dose, HbA1c, and BMI z-score, patients with SCH had significantly higher levels of total cholesterol (178.7 vs 175.3 mg/dl, P<0.001) and LDL-cholesterol (97.0 vs 93.7 mg/dl, P<0.001) compared with euthyroid patients. We concluded that SCH is a common finding in children, adolescents, and young adults with T1DM. SCH is associated with increased levels of total cholesterol, and LDL-cholesterol adjusted for potential confounders. SCH-associated increases in lipid and lipoprotein levels may therefore add to an increased long-term cardiovascular risk in young patients with T1DM.

A retrospective case control study was performed in order to explore the effect of subclinical hypothyroidism on metabolic control in Type 1 diabetes mellitus. For this purpose each patient with Type 1 diabetes and subclinical hypothyroidism (cases) was matched for age, duration of disease and, if possible, for sex, with two to three diabetic patients without hypothyroidism (controls). Parameters of metabolic control such as HbA1c, total insulin requirement and frequency of symptomatic hypoglycaemia were retrieved for 12, 6 and 3 months before and after diagnosis of hypothyroidism. Thirteen patients (two male/11 female) patients were diagnosed with subclinical hypothyroidism and were matched with 31 controls (nine male/22 female). There was no difference (mean and range) in terms of age (11.9 years (4.4-18.1) vs. 11.7 years (3.5-18.1), P = 0.9) and duration of disease (5.1 years (1.2-10.5) vs. 4.38 years (0.9-10.8), P = 0.6) between the two groups. There was no difference in HbA1c and total insulin requirement between the two groups at any time point of assessment (anova P = 0.8 and P = 0.1, respectively). Patients with hypothyroidism had significantly more symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes during the 12 months before diagnosis (anova P = 0.05), increasing progressively during this time period and reaching a peak at time 0 (5.5+/-0.4 vs. 1.6+/-0.1 episodes/month, P = 0.01). No difference could be detected within 6 months of starting substitution therapy (2.4+/-0.2 vs. 1.6+/-0.1 episodes/week, P = 0.8). We concluded that these data suggest that subclinical hypothyroidism is associated with an increased risk of symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
passage_3: "Predictivity of thyroid autoantibodies for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes" investigates the prevalence of thyroid autoantibodies and their significance for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes. Antibodies to thyroglobulin (anti-TG) and thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) were measured in 216 patients (113 boys; median age 12.9 years (range 1-22 years)) with Type 1 diabetes (diabetes duration 2.5 years (0-14 years)) in a cross-sectional study. Sixteen patients with significantly elevated anti-TPO titres were followed longitudinally (6.0 years (4-13 years)) including the measurement of anti-TPO, anti-TG, T(3), T(4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ultrasound assessment. Twenty-two patients (10.0%) had significantly elevated titres of anti-TPO, 19 (8.7%) of anti-TG and 13 (5.9%) of both autoantibodies. Girls had more frequently elevated anti-TPO antibodies than boys (P < 0.05). Eight of 16 patients (50%) developed thyroid disorders defined by a TSH elevation (> or = 4.5 microU/ml) and/or sonographic thyroid abnormalities during a median time of 3.5 years (2-6 years) after first detection of anti-TPO positivity. They were characterized by higher levels of anti-TPO (P = 0.001) and a more frequent coexistence of anti-TG antibodies (P = 0.002) than those with no development of thyroid disorder even after an observation period of 5.5 years (5-10 years). We concluded that because 50% of children with diabetes and significant titres of anti-TPO develop thyroid problems within 3-4 years, examinations of thyroid antibodies should be performed yearly. In cases of significant antibody titres, thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment are recommended in order to minimize the risk of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in these patients.

question: What was the cost-effectiveness of the intervention in the Subclinical Hypothyroidism and Dyslipidemia in Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.txt study?
passage_1: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

In response to concerns regarding the generalizability of their original findings, the authors note that historical clinical trial cohorts remain relevant, address changes in retinal photography methods (such as shifting from seven-field to one- or two-field screening), and emphasize that data-driven, personalized screening intervals offer an effective and cost-saving alternative to universal annual exams without compromising patient care.

A randomised controlled trial evaluates the impact of a six-month exercise program on glycemic control, plasma lipid levels, blood pressure, hypoglycemia frequency, anthropometric measurements, and insulin requirements among 196 adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus. The findings reveal that regular exercise significantly improves glycemic control by reducing HbA1c levels, decreases dyslipidemia (lowering total cholesterol, LDL-C, and triglycerides while increasing HDL-C), reduces daily insulin dosage requirements, and leads to beneficial reductions in body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference without increasing the frequency of hypoglycemic attacks. Based on these results, the paper concludes and recommends that exercise should be considered an indispensable therapeutic component in the medical management of adolescents with type 1 diabetes to optimize glycemic control and mitigate cardiovascular risk factors.

question: What were the main findings of the Systematic Review Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes.txt systematic review?

passage_1: "Teen-Longitudinal Assessment of Bariatric Surgery (Teen-LABS): Methodologic Features of the First Prospective Multicenter Study of Adolescent Bariatric Surgery" evaluates the methodological design and protocol of the first prospective, multicenter observational study designed to collect coordinated clinical, epidemiological, and behavioral data on adolescents (≤19 years old) undergoing bariatric surgery compared to adult historical counterparts. The paper outlines the study findings regarding protocol structure, noting that 200 adolescent patients across four clinical centers and a comparison group of 200 adults across five centers will be tracked to determine baseline differences in health status, evaluate early (30-day) and intermediate-term (1–2 year) surgical risks, and compare psychosocial domains including eating behaviors, depressive symptoms, and health-related quality of life. The paper provides guidelines for ancillary study proposals, specifying that external researchers may utilize Teen-LABS data or biospecimens provided their protocols do not interfere with the observational nature of the core study and receive approval following established submission procedures.
passage_2: "Cardiovascular Risk Factors in Severely Obese Adolescents: The Teen Longitudinal Assessment of Bariatric Surgery (Teen-LABS) Study" evaluates the preoperative prevalence and predictors of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors among severely obese adolescents undergoing weight-loss surgery across five centers in the United States. Analyzing a cohort of 242 participants, the study found a high baseline prevalence of CVD risk factors, including fasting hyperinsulinemia (74%), elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels (75%), dyslipidemia (50%), elevated blood pressure (49%), impaired fasting glucose levels (26%), and diabetes mellitus (14%). Furthermore, increased body mass index (BMI) significantly correlated with a higher risk of impaired fasting glucose, elevated blood pressure, and elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels, while male sex was associated with a greater likelihood of dyslipidemia and elevated blood pressure. Based on these findings, the study highlights that even among severely obese adolescents, the recognition and targeted clinical management of specific CVD risk factors are crucial to help limit the further progression of cardiovascular disease.
passage_3: "Comparison of Surgical and Medical Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes in Severely Obese Adolescents" evaluates the two-year outcomes of glycemic control, body mass index, blood pressure, lipid profiles, kidney function, and clinical adverse events in severely obese adolescents with type 2 diabetes undergoing bariatric surgery compared to those receiving medical therapy. The study found that surgical intervention led to a significant decrease in mean hemoglobin A1c concentration from 6.8% to 5.5% and a 29% reduction in body mass index, accompanied by marked improvements in blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and kidney function, whereas medical therapy resulted in increased hemoglobin A1c from 6.4% to 7.8%, a 3.7% increase in body mass index, and worsening or unchanged risk factors, though 23% of surgical patients required subsequent operations for complications. Based on these findings, the paper recommends conducting a well-designed, prospective controlled study to further define the precise role, long-term health, and surgical outcomes of metabolic surgery for adolescents with type 2 diabetes.

question: What were the main findings of the The  Type 1 Diabetes Exercise Initiative Pediatric (T1DEXIP) Study.txt study?

passage_1: The American Diabetes Association position statement on Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents emphasizes that pediatric-onset diabetes requires distinct clinical strategies because children are not simply small adults. The disease differs significantly from adult diabetes in its epidemiology, pathophysiology, developmental impact, and response to therapy, meaning care must continuously adapt to match a child's evolving growth stages. The statement outlines a standardized three-stage continuum for disease progression, starting with Stage 1 (presymptomatic with multiple islet autoantibodies and normoglycemia), moving to Stage 2 (presymptomatic with autoantibodies and dysglycemia), and concluding with Stage 3 (symptomatic clinical onset due to insulin deficiency). To manage the condition effectively, diagnosis must be pursued expeditiously to prevent rapid clinical deterioration and diabetic ketoacidosis. Clinicians are advised to differentiate Type 1 diabetes from Type 2, monogenic forms, and atypical presentations using autoantibody panels, family history, and C-peptide testing, while consulting pediatric endocrinologists in ambiguous situations such as stress hyperglycemia. For blood glucose management, the guidelines strongly recommend intensive insulin regimens delivered via multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pumps). Across pediatric age groups, the recommended target A1C level is set at under 7.5%, though this should be tailored based on individual risks like hypoglycemia. Finally, comprehensive care requires monitoring blood glucose multiple times daily, leveraging continuous glucose monitoring systems, and testing blood ketones during acute illness or unexpected hyperglycemia.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.
