question: What were the main findings of the The Effect of a Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial on Lifestyle Behaviors Among Families at Risk for Developing Type 2 Diabetes Across Europe The Feel4Diabetes Study.txt rct?
passage_1: "The effect of a cluster-randomized controlled trial on lifestyle behaviors among families at risk for developing type 2 diabetes across Europe: the Feel4Diabetes-study" investigated the effect of the Feel4Diabetes-intervention, a 2-year multilevel intervention, on energy balance-related behaviors among European families at risk for developing type 2 diabetes. Intervention effects on self-reported physical activity, sedentary behavior and eating behaviors were investigated across and within the participating countries: Belgium, Finland, Greece, Spain, Hungary and Bulgaria. Families were recruited through schools, located in low socio-economic status areas. In total, 4484 families at risk for developing type 2 diabetes were selected using the FINDRISC-questionnaire. Parents' and children's energy balance-related behaviors data were collected by questionnaires at three time points (baseline, mid- and post intervention). Families assigned to the intervention group were invited to participate in a 2-year school-, community-, and family-based intervention to promote a healthier lifestyle, including counseling sessions (first intervention year) and text messages (second intervention year). Families assigned to the control group received standard care, including medical check-up results and recommendations and tips regarding a healthy lifestyle. To assess the intervention-effects, Mixed Models were conducted using the R-Package "lmer "with R v3.2. Significant intervention effects were found on a certain number of families' lifestyle behaviors. Significant favorable intervention effects were detected on parents' water consumption and consumption of fruit and vegetables, and on children's consumption of sweets and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
passage_2: "A Clinical Trial to Maintain Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 2 Diabetes (TODAY)” study evaluates the efficacy of three treatment regimens—metformin alone, metformin combined with rosiglitazone, and metformin combined with an intensive lifestyle-intervention program—in achieving durable glycemic control among children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes. The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that metformin plus rosiglitazone was particularly effective in girls, while metformin monotherapy was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants. Serious adverse events occurred in 19.2% of participants across the trial, and although the paper does not explicitly state formal clinical recommendations or guidelines, it concludes that metformin monotherapy fails to maintain durable glycemic control in roughly half of youth with type 2 diabetes and that adding rosiglitazone provides superior glycemic durability compared to monotherapy or intensive lifestyle interventions.
passage_3: "Efficacy and safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin versus placebo and the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin versus placebo in young people with type 2 diabetes (DINAMO): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel group, phase 3 trial" reported that the incidence of type 2 diabetes in young people is increasing, but treatments remain limited. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of an empagliflozin dosing regimen versus placebo and linagliptin versus placebo on glycaemic control in young people with type 2 diabetes. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial done in 108 centres in 15 countries, participants with type 2 diabetes (aged 10-17 years; HbA1c 6·5-10·5% [48-91 mmol/mol]) who had been previously treated with metformin or insulin were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to oral empagliflozin 10 mg, oral linagliptin 5 mg, or placebo. Participants in the empagliflozin group who did not have HbA1c below 7·0% (<53 mmol/mol) by week 12 underwent a second double-blinded randomisation (1:1) at week 14, either remaining on 10 mg or increasing to 25 mg. Participants in the placebo group were randomly reassigned (1:1:1) in a double-blinded manner at week 26 to linagliptin 5 mg or one of the empagliflozin doses (10 mg or 25 mg). Investigators were masked throughout the trial and received assignments of blinded medication kits through interactive response technology for all participants at the initial randomisation and for the re-randomisations at weeks 14 and 26. The primary outcome was change from baseline in HbA1c at 26 weeks. For empagliflozin, results were based on a pooled analysis for all participants on empagliflozin. Safety was assessed until week 52. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03429543. Between April 26, 2018, and May 26, 2022, of 262 screened participants, 158 (60%) were randomly assigned to treatment (53 [34%] to placebo, 52 [33%] to empagliflozin 10 mg, and 53 [34%] to linagliptin).

Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

Among 1,206 screened participants with an overweight or obese phenotype, 9.8% tested positive for islet autoantibodies (5.9% single-antibody positive and 3.9% double-antibody positive), with autoantibody positivity being significantly more frequent in white and male participants. The study finds that if 2017 incidence levels remain constant, youth diabetes cases will increase from 213,000 in 2017 (185,000 type 1; 28,000 type 2) to 239,000 in 2060 (191,000 type 1; 48,000 type 2), reflecting a 3% relative rise for type 1 and a 69% relative rise for type 2 diabetes. However, if the increasing incidence trends observed between 2002 and 2017 persist, total youth diabetes cases are projected to reach 526,000 by 2060 (306,000 type 1; 220,000 type 2)—representing a 65% relative increase for type 1 and a 673% relative increase for type 2 diabetes—with substantial widening of racial and ethnic disparities leading to the highest prevalence among non-Hispanic Black youth. Under a baseline scenario with constant incidence rates, the projected number of youth with T1DM increases from 166,018 in 2010 to 203,385 in 2050, while youth with T2DM increases from 20,203 to 30,111, both driven primarily by demographic growth among racial and ethnic minority populations. Based on these findings, the paper recommends urgent public health action to curb these potential increases, calling for additional research into effective T2DM primary prevention strategies aimed at youth obesity and high-risk groups, alongside enhanced health care system planning and expanded medical workforce training to manage the growing pediatric diabetes burden.

Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.

passage_1: The study Social Determinants of Health and Diabetes: A Scientific Review evaluates the literature on the associations of five key social determinants of health (SDOH)—socioeconomic status, neighborhood and physical environment, food environment, health care, and social context—with diabetes risk and health outcomes, as well as the impact of interventions targeting these factors. Findings indicate that lower income, lower educational attainment, housing instability, food insecurity, and poor healthcare access are consistently associated with higher diabetes prevalence, greater risk of complications, worse glycemic control, and increased mortality, with widening disparities over time. While direct interventions on structural socioeconomic factors remain understudied, literacy-adapted education and health-literacy tools show small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control (HbA1c). Based on these findings, the paper recommends strengthening linkages between healthcare systems and community-based sectors, expanding diabetes research to evaluate multi-level structural interventions targeting SDOH, and providing evidence-based guidelines to inform clinical practice and policy toward achieving health equity.
passage_2: The study "Mental health comorbidity and youth onset type 2 diabetes: A systematic review of the literature" evaluates the current literature surrounding youth with depression and type 2 diabetes (T2D), specifically reviewing 13 publications from 8 studies involving 2,244 individuals aged 6 to 17. The findings indicate that while depressive symptoms are common in youth with T2D and correlate with negative T2D outcomes, most studies failed to formally assess for major depressive disorder (MDD) and actively excluded participants with a prior MDD diagnosis. Based on these gaps, the authors recommend that future research focus on four key areas: including youth with diagnosed MDD, conducting treatment studies addressing both T2D and MDD concurrently, analyzing larger and more racially diverse youth samples, and evaluating how social determinants of health alongside mental health comorbidities impact T2D outcomes.
passage_3: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study Group evaluated changes in the prevalence of physician-diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes among children and adolescents under age 20 across six US regions between 2001, 2009, and 2017. Utilizing a cross-sectional observational design, researchers assessed a mean population of 3.47 million youths per prevalence year to determine shifts in youth-onset diabetes rates over time across various demographic groups. Over the 16-year period, estimated prevalence increased significantly for both conditions. Type 1 diabetes prevalence among youths aged 19 and under rose from 1.48 per 1,000 in 2001 to 2.15 per 1,000 in 2017, representing a 45.1% relative increase, with the largest absolute gains occurring among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black youths. Type 2 diabetes prevalence among adolescents aged 10 to 19 nearly doubled, rising from 0.34 per 1,000 in 2001 to 0.67 per 1,000 in 2017—a 95.3% relative increase—with non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic youths experiencing the greatest absolute increases. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. Furthermore, the study notes that understanding these demographic trends is essential for targeting clinical interventions and public health efforts toward the specific racial and ethnic groups facing the steepest rises in disease burden.

passage_1: "Transfer from pediatric to adult health care: effects on diabetes outcomes" evaluates the impact of transitioning from pediatric to adult diabetes care on emerging adults with type 1 diabetes, focusing on outcomes such as diabetes care visit attendance, glycemic control, and acute diabetes-related complications while assessing the methodological strength of existing observational and interventional studies. The paper's findings indicate that while observational studies often report a decline in diabetes care visit frequency alongside an improvement or no change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) after transfer, these results are heavily limited by methodological flaws, including incomplete data, high dropout rates among patients who drop out of follow-up, lack of appropriate comparison groups, and confounding physical and psychosocial maturation. Furthermore, studies tracking patients who left the pediatric health system for a broad array of adult providers found deterioration in glycemic control compared to peers remaining in pediatric care, and structured transition interventions showed temporary benefits in clinic attendance or HbA1c that were often not sustained long-term. Regarding recommendations and guidelines, the paper does not propose new clinical guidelines or structured transition protocols; instead, it highlights a critical lack of methodologically strong empirical evidence—noting that most current recommendations are based on expert consensus or clinical experience—and emphasizes that future research must address these shortcomings by utilizing proper comparison groups, tracking patients across diverse adult care settings, and accounting for patient attrition to properly guide clinicians and improve emerging adult care.
passage_2: The study “Screening eye exams in youth with type 1 diabetes under 18 years of age: once may be enough?” evaluates the optimal frequency and necessity of eye screening examinations in pediatric patients under 18 years of age with type 1 diabetes, drawing on long-term data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) research group. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

question: What were the main findings of the The TODAY2.txt study?
passage_1: “Retinopathy in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes Participating in the TODAY Clinical Trial” evaluates the prevalence of diabetic retinopathy in a cohort of 517 youth (aged 10–17 years at baseline) with type 2 diabetes of 2 to 8 years duration using standardized central grading of fundus photographs. The study found an overall retinopathy prevalence of 13.7%, with all affected participants exhibiting mild or very mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and no cases of macular edema or proliferative disease. Retinopathy risk was significantly higher among participants who were older, had a longer diabetes duration, or had higher mean HbA1c levels, whereas those in the highest body mass index (BMI) tertile unexpectedly presented with a lower prevalence. Although specific clinical recommendations and guidelines were not provided, the authors note that the natural history and progression of diabetic retinopathy in youth with type 2 diabetes will be further clarified through continued follow-up of this cohort.
passage_2: The TODAY2 study evaluates the prevalence and associated factors of high diabetes distress among young adults with youth-onset type 2 diabetes. Analyzing 438 participants, the researchers found that 24% reported high overall diabetes distress, with 40% experiencing high regimen distress and 29.7% experiencing high emotional burden. High distress was significantly associated with female sex, higher HbA1c levels, moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms, and a lack of healthcare coverage, while moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were linked to both regimen distress and emotional burden, and insulin treatment was specifically linked to emotional burden. The paper recommends that future research focus on identifying modifiable factors associated with high diabetes distress in order to inform targeted psychosocial interventions for this medically vulnerable group.
passage_3: The “Characteristics of adolescents and youth with recent-onset type 2 diabetes: the TODAY cohort at baseline” evaluates the baseline demographic, clinical, medical history, and biochemical characteristics of 704 American adolescents and youth aged 10 to 17 years who were diagnosed with recent-onset type 2 diabetes for less than two years and had a body mass index at or above the 85th percentile. The findings reveal that the participant group was predominantly female (64.9%), had a mean age of 14.0 years, and consisted mostly of racial and ethnic minority populations, including 41.1% Hispanic and 31.5% non-Hispanic Black youth, with 89.4% having a family history of diabetes and significant socioeconomic challenges such as 41.5% residing in households earning less than $25,000 annually. Furthermore, clinical and biochemical comorbidities were highly prevalent within two years of diagnosis, including low high-density lipoprotein levels in 79.8%, blood pressure at or above the 90th percentile in 26.3%, microalbuminuria in 13.0%, and elevated triglycerides in 10.2% of participants. The study does not explicitly provide formal clinical practice guidelines or recommendations, but it emphasizes that youth-onset type 2 diabetes presents with substantial risk factors and metabolic abnormalities early in the course of the disease.

The study found that maximal glucose drops occurred 8 to 16 hours after exercise, with larger drops during activity being associated with lower mean glucose levels immediately post-exercise and 12 to 16 hours later; overall, nocturnal hypoglycemia occurred on 14% of post-exercise nights (compared to 12% on sedentary days), with significantly higher rates when average total daily activity was at least 60 minutes, during longer individual exercise sessions, in youth with longer diabetes duration or lower HbA1c, with conventional pump use, and when time below range was at least 4% in the preceding 24 hours. While explicit clinical guidelines were not provided in the paper, the authors highlight that regular physical activity should be prescribed and encouraged for youth with type 1 diabetes (matching the general pediatric recommendation of 60 minutes daily) and recommend leveraging these participant- and event-level findings to inform new clinical guidelines, decision support tools, and refined automated closed-loop insulin delivery algorithms to better mitigate exercise-related hypoglycemia.
passage_2: The study titled Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Physical Activity in Pediatric Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis evaluates the magnitude, precision, and constancy of differences in cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and daily physical activity levels between children/adolescents aged 18 years or younger with type 1 diabetes (T1D) or type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their peers without diabetes. question: What were the main findings of the Thyroid and Islet Autoantibodies Predict Autoimmune Thyroid Disease at Type 1 Diabetes Diagnosis.txt study?
passage_1: "Thyroid autoimmunity in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus" reviews the incidence and evidence for screening for thyroid autoimmunity and thyroid dysfunction in Type 1 diabetes. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria were prospective cohort studies screening for thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction (defined as an abnormal thyroid-stimulating hormone level) in Type 1 diabetes. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction before diabetes onset. Outcomes examined were: incidence of thyroid autoimmunity and/or dysfunction; association between thyroid autoimmunity and dysfunction; and cost-effectiveness. Data sources were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, manual searching and contact with authors, with limitations to English language and human studies. Meta-analysis was performed using random effects models. We identified 14 eligible studies, involving 2972 young people and 789 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Follow-up ranged from 1-18 years. None of the studies were of good methodological quality (Newcastle Ottowa Scale score > 7). The incidence of thyroid dysfunction (11 studies) ranged from 27 (95% CI 15-45) to 246 (95% CI 118-453) per 10 000 patient-years and thyroid autoimmunity (four studies) from 13 (95% CI 0.3-71) to 326 (95% CI 194-510). The risk of thyroid dysfunction was higher in those with thyroid autoimmunity: summary risk ratio 25 (95% CI 9-71) and was higher in children (49, 95% CI 16-150) compared with adults (7, 95% CI 3-13). No studies examined cost-effectiveness of screening. We concluded that there is a markedly increased risk of thyroid dysfunction in people with Type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoimmunity. The optimal method or frequency of screening could not be determined from available data. Future studies should examine whether screening improves clinical outcomes in this population.
passage_2: "Predictivity of thyroid autoantibodies for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes" investigates the prevalence of thyroid autoantibodies and their significance for the development of thyroid disorders in children and adolescents with Type 1 diabetes. Antibodies to thyroglobulin (anti-TG) and thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) were measured in 216 patients (113 boys; median age 12.9 years (range 1-22 years)) with Type 1 diabetes (diabetes duration 2.5 years (0-14 years)) in a cross-sectional study. Sixteen patients with significantly elevated anti-TPO titres were followed longitudinally (6.0 years (4-13 years)) including the measurement of anti-TPO, anti-TG, T(3), T(4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and ultrasound assessment. Twenty-two patients (10.0%) had significantly elevated titres of anti-TPO, 19 (8.7%) of anti-TG and 13 (5.9%) of both autoantibodies. Girls had more frequently elevated anti-TPO antibodies than boys (P < 0.05). Eight of 16 patients (50%) developed thyroid disorders defined by a TSH elevation (> or = 4.5 microU/ml) and/or sonographic thyroid abnormalities during a median time of 3.5 years (2-6 years) after first detection of anti-TPO positivity. They were characterized by higher levels of anti-TPO (P = 0.001) and a more frequent coexistence of anti-TG antibodies (P = 0.002) than those with no development of thyroid disorder even after an observation period of 5.5 years (5-10 years). We concluded that because 50% of children with diabetes and significant titres of anti-TPO develop thyroid problems within 3-4 years, examinations of thyroid antibodies should be performed yearly. In cases of significant antibody titres, thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment are recommended in order to minimize the risk of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in these patients.
passage_3: This perspective article from Diabetes Care, titled Adult-Onset Type 1 Diabetes: Current Understanding and Challenges, summarizes the outcomes of an international JDRF expert workshop aimed at improving the clinical understanding, diagnostic accuracy, and management of adult-onset type 1 diabetes. The primary objective of the workshop and paper is to address the widespread issue of misdiagnosis, as over half of all new type 1 diabetes cases occur in adults, yet nearly 40% are initially misclassified—most commonly as type 2 diabetes due to slower metabolic progression and overlapping clinical traits. By highlighting the distinct epidemiological, immunogenetic, and metabolic features of adult-onset cases, the authors seek to establish clearer diagnostic frameworks and treatment guidelines for practicing clinicians. To evaluate potential cases effectively, the authors provide the diagnostic "AABBCC" framework, guiding clinicians to systematically assess Age at onset, Autoimmunity via islet autoantibody testing, Body habitus and BMI, family and personal background, glycemic Control trajectory, and associated Comorbidities such as thyroid autoimmunity or celiac disease. For laboratory guidelines, the authors recommend ordering islet autoantibody assays as the primary test for short-duration disease (under three years), with serum glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies serving as the predominant marker. For disease durations exceeding three years, C-peptide testing paired with blood glucose is recommended as the main tool to measure remaining beta-cell function. Regarding therapeutic management, the paper outlines guidelines based on C-peptide levels and disease characteristics. Patients with random C-peptide levels at or below 300 pmol/L require primary insulin therapy.

The study found that 45.6% of participants experienced treatment failure over an average follow-up of 3.86 years, with metformin plus rosiglitazone demonstrating superiority over metformin alone by reducing treatment failure to 38.6% compared to 51.7% for monotherapy, whereas metformin plus lifestyle intervention yielded intermediate results (46.6%) that were not significantly different from metformin alone. While the primary study was strictly epidemiological and did not issue formal clinical practice guidelines or actionable policy recommendations, it highlights the critical need to anticipate and allocate clinical resources to manage the growing burden of youth-onset diabetes. The authors analyzed retinopathy progression in youth to determine whether repeated annual eye exams in early adolescence provide significant clinical benefit or if less frequent screening is sufficient. The findings demonstrate that retinopathy in youth under 18 with type 1 diabetes is exceedingly rare and generally mild when present, suggesting that frequent annual eye examinations in this younger demographic may offer minimal added value. Based on these findings, the study provides recommendations and guidelines suggesting that eye screening once during adolescence—rather than annual exams starting shortly after diagnosis—may be adequate for low-risk youth with type 1 diabetes until they reach adulthood or develop longer diabetes duration.

question: What were the main findings of the Treatment With Canagliflozin Versus Placebo in Children and Adolescents With Type 2 Diabetes A Randomized Clinical Trial.txt rct?
passage_1: "Treatment with canagliflozin versus placebo in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes: a randomized clinical trial" reported that treatment options for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are limited. Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor approved for the treatment of T2DM in adults. The objective was to assess the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin in children and adolescents with T2DM. This was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03170518; EudraCT: 2016-005223-88) conducted at 104 sites in 10 countries. Participants were children and adolescents aged 10 years or older with T2DM (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] ≥6.5% to ≤11%). Participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (100 mg) or placebo once daily. Participants with week 12 readings of 7% or higher for HbA1c and at least 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomly assigned again at week 13 to either keep receiving 100 mg of canagliflozin (or placebo) or have their dose uptitrated to 300 mg (or placebo). The treatment period was 52 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, along with secondary efficacy end points and safety. A total of 171 participants were randomly assigned to canagliflozin (n = 84) or placebo (n = 87). At week 26, HbA1c reduction from baseline was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (difference in least-squares means, -0.76% [95% CI, -1.25% to -0.27%]; P = 0.002). The proportion of participants who achieved HbA1c levels below 6.5% was significantly greater with canagliflozin than placebo (36.3% vs. 14.0%; difference, 22.3 percentage points [CI, 10.5 to 34.1 percentage points]). Treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs) occurred in 77.4% and 74.7% and serious treatment-emergent AEs in 9.5% and 5.7% of participants who received canagliflozin and placebo, respectively.
passage_2: "Efficacy and safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin versus placebo and the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin versus placebo in youth with type 2 diabetes: a multicentre, randomised, doubleblind, parallel group, phase 3 trial" evaluates the efficacy and safety of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin (10 mg or 25 mg daily) and the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin (5 mg daily) compared to a shared placebo over 26 weeks in youth aged 10–17 years with type 2 diabetes who were previously treated with metformin and/or insulin. The study found that empagliflozin provided a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in HbA1c baseline levels compared to placebo (-0.84%, p=0.012), whereas linagliptin did not show a statistically significant reduction (-0.34%, p=0.29). Hypoglycemia was the most frequently reported adverse event, with higher rates observed in active treatment groups, though no severe hypoglycemia cases occurred. Based on these findings, the paper suggests that empagliflozin may offer a valuable new oral treatment option for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes to address the therapeutic unmet need in this population.
passage_3: "Efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in children and young adults with type 2 diabetes: a prospective, multicentre, randomised, parallel group, phase 3 study" reported that since there are few treatment options for young people with type 2 diabetes, we aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin as add-on therapy in children, adolescents, and young adults with type 2 diabetes receiving metformin, insulin, or both. This multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised phase 3 study was undertaken at 30 centres in five countries (Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Russia, and the USA). Participants aged 10-24 years with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c concentration of 6·5-11% (48-97 mmol/mol) were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo during a 24 week double-blind period, which was then followed by a 28 week open-label safety extension in which all participants received dapagliflozin. Participants and study personnel were masked and participants were randomly assigned treatment (placebo or study drug) using an interactive web and voice response system. The primary outcome was between-group differences in change in HbA1c concentration from baseline to 24 weeks (intention-to-treat analysis). A prespecified sensitivity analysis of the primary outcome was also assessed in the per-protocol population, which included only protocol-compliant participants. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02725593. Between June 22, 2016, and March 15, 2019, 72 participants (19 [26%] of whom were aged 18-24 years) were randomly assigned (39 to dapagliflozin and 33 to placebo). Mean age was 16·1 (SD 3·3) years. In the intention-to-treat analysis, after 24 weeks, mean change in HbA1c concentration was -0·25% (95% CI -0·85 to 0·34; -2·7 [-9·3 to 3·7] mmol/mol) for dapagliflozin and 0·50% (-0·18 to 1·17; 5·5 [-2·0 to 12·8] mmol/mol) for placebo. The between-group difference was -0·75% (95% CI -1·65 to 0·15; -8·2 [-18·0 to 1·6] mmol/mol; p=0·10).

Older age, lower baseline glycosylated hemoglobin, and higher parental education were independently associated with increased odds of transitioning. Importantly, transferring from pediatric to adult care was associated with a 2.5-fold increase in the odds of having poor glycemic control (hemoglobin A1c ≥9%) at follow-up, alongside other risk factors such as nonwhite race/ethnicity and higher baseline hemoglobin A1c. Based on these findings, the study highlights that young adults require additional support during their move to adult medical care. Furthermore, referencing guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Physicians, the American Academy of Family Practice, and the American Diabetes Association, the paper notes that all young adults with diabetes should transition to adult-oriented medical care between 18 and 21 years of age.

The findings indicate that out of 182 participants, 56% transferred to adult care, 15% received no care, and 29% remained in pediatric care, with higher age at diagnosis and longer diabetes duration predicting the departure from pediatric care. Furthermore, transferring to adult care or receiving no care was significantly associated with higher odds of poor glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥ 9.0%), independent of sex, race, ethnicity, or baseline HbA1c levels. Recommendations and guidelines provided in the paper emphasize the urgent need for tailored clinical programs, healthcare system policies, targeted treatments, patient-centered care, and early education for both adult specialists and generalists to support the growing population of young adults with youth-onset Type 2 diabetes and prevent disease deterioration during the transition period.

The paper's findings indicate that early transition can lead to worse glycemic control, reduced annual clinic visits, and high rates of care lapses, while a gradual transition approach and retention in specialty adult endocrinology care help mitigate these risks. Regarding recommendations and guidelines, professional organizations such as the American Diabetes Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics advise initiating transition preparation at least one year prior to transfer (or as early as ages 12–13), systematically assessing transition readiness using validated tools or diabetes-specific checklists, gradually shifting diabetes management responsibilities from parents to the patient, providing specific adult care provider referrals, and routinely screening for both microvascular/macrovascular complications and psychosocial issues such as depression and disordered eating.

Another comparison group was adults undergoing gastric bypass at the same institution during the same time period. Body weight decreased from 133 kg (SD = 22) at inclusion to 92 kg (SD = 17) after 1 year and was 89 (SD = 18) after 2 years (p < 0·001) representing a 32% (-35 to -30) weight loss after 2 years, corresponding to 76% (-81 to -71) excess weight loss. Significant improvement in cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors and inflammation was seen after surgery. The treatment was generally well tolerated and quality of life improved significantly. The surgical adverse events included cholecystectomies (10%) and operations for internal hernia (9%) but no postoperative mortality. Adolescents undergoing laparoscopic gastric bypass surgery achieve similar weight loss to adults. Improvements in risk factors and quality of life were substantial. Weithorn evaluates the role of minors' legal competence in American healthcare decision-making, examining the default doctrine of parental consent alongside statutory and judicial exceptions such as the mature minor doctrine. The analysis finds that a minor's decisional competence is rarely the primary trigger for transferring legal authority; instead, courts and legislatures first assess whether policy goals or constitutional rights justify bypassing parental authority before assessing whether capable minors should decide for themselves. Furthermore, psychological and neuroscientific research indicates that cognitive capacities necessary for logical "cold cognition" reasoning reach adult levels by early to mid-adolescence (around ages 12 to 15), while psychosocial maturity in emotional "hot cognition" contexts continues to develop into adulthood. Based on these findings, the author recommends recognizing that legal authority rules reflect deliberate policy balances rather than simple reflections of developmental maturity, and guidelines emphasize promoting minors' participation as collaborative partners in medical decisions alongside parents and healthcare providers, regardless of strict legal boundaries

The paper finds that basic and translational neuroscience accounts for approximately 85% of the NIMH non-HIV/AIDS budget, leaving only around 15% for services and interventions research, despite substantial immediate public health needs and high rates of unmet mental health care. The authors recommend a rebalancing and diversification of the mental health research portfolio to allocate greater funding toward scalable, cost-efficient interventions, implementation science, suicide prevention, and addressing social determinants of health. question: What were the main findings of the Younger Age at Onset and Sex Predict Celiac Disease in Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes An Italian Multicenter Study.txt study?
passage_1: "Younger age at onset and sex predict celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: an Italian multicenter study" estimates the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in Italian children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and to assess whether age at onset of type 1 diabetes is independently associated with diagnosis of celiac disease. The study group was a clinic-based cohort of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes cared for in 25 Italian centers for childhood diabetes. Yearly screening for celiac disease was performed using IgA/IgG anti-gliadin and IgA anti-endomysium antibodies. Of the 4,322 children and adolescents (age 11.8 ± 4.2 years) identified with type 1 diabetes, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was diagnosed in 292 (prevalence 6.8%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–7.6), with a higher risk seen in girls than in boys (odds ratio [OR] 1.93, 1.51–2.47). In 89% of these, diabetes was diagnosed before celiac disease. In logistic regression analyses, being younger at onset of diabetes, being female, and having a diagnosis of a thyroid disorder were independently associated with the risk of having diabetes and celiac disease. In comparison with subjects who were older than 9 years at onset of diabetes, subjects who were younger than 4 years at onset had an OR of 3.27 (2.20–4.85). We have provided evidence that 1) the prevalence of biopsy-confirmed celiac disease in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes is high (6.8%); 2) the risk of having both diseases is threefold higher in children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age <4 years than in those age >9 years; and 3) girls have a higher risk of having both diseases than boys.

The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). question: What were the long-term outcomes beyond the study period in the Younger Age at Onset and Sex Predict Celiac Disease in Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes An Italian Multicenter Study.txt study?
passage_1: "Celiac disease in children with type 1 diabetes varies around the world: an international, cross-sectional study of 57 375 patients from the SWEET registry" reports that children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at much higher risk of developing celiac disease (CD) than the general population. The aim of the study was to assess the prevalence and differences in clinical presentation of CD in T1D in different regions of the world. This study is based on the Better control in Pediatric and Adolescent diabeteS: Working to crEate cEnTers of Reference (SWEET) database. There were 57 375 patients included in the study, aged ≤18 years from 54 SWEET centers. Only centers with screening for celiac disease were included. Regression models adjusted for age, diabetes duration, and gender and a fixed effect in the models for region was used. Diabetes duration, age at diabetes onset, and sex were presented as unadjusted results. CD was present in 2652 subjects (4.5%), with different prevalence among regions: from 1.9% in Asia/Middle East to 6.9% in Australia/New Zealand. CD was observed more often among females. Comparing children with and without CD, characteristics for those with CD were younger age at diabetes onset (6.3 [3.3; 9.8] vs 8.1 [4.6; 11.3], P < 0.001) and had longer diabetes duration (6.4 [3.6; 9.8] vs 4.8 [2.1; 8.2], P < 0.001). Further, they had lower glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in Europe and North America/Canada; lower body mass index (BMI)-SD score (BMI-SDS) in southern Europe, North America, and Canada; In most regions daily insulin dose was lower, height-SDS was lower, and the percentage of insulin pump users was higher in children with T1D and CD. We concluded that the prevalence and the anthropometric and metabolic consequences of CD in children with T1D differ around the world.
passage_2: "Screening for celiac disease in type 1 diabetes: a systematic review" reports that prevalence rates of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and celiac disease (CD) vary from 1.6% to 16.4% worldwide. Screening guidelines are variable and not evidence based. Our aim was to conduct a systematic review of CD in T1D. Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Studies were limited to those in English and in humans. We selected longitudinal cohort studies screening for CD in T1D with at least 5 years of follow-up. Screening rates, characteristics, and prevalence of biopsy-proven CD in people with T1D were extracted. We identified 457 nonduplicate citations; 48 were selected for full-text review. Nine longitudinal cohort studies in 11 157 children and adolescents with 587 cases of biopsy-proven CD met the inclusion criteria. Median follow-up was 10 years (range: 5–18 years). The weighted pooled prevalence of CD was 5.1% (95% confidence interval: 3.1–7.4%). After excluding 41 cases with CD onset before T1D, CD was diagnosed in 218 of 546 (40%) subjects within 1 year, in 55% within 2 years, and in 79% within 5 years of diabetes duration. Two studies (478 cases) reported higher rates of CD in children aged <5 years at T1D diagnosis. The duration of follow-up varied across the included studies. CD screening frequency progressively decreased with increased T1D duration. We concluded that because most cases of CD are diagnosed within 5 years of T1D diagnosis, screening should be considered at T1D diagnosis and within 2 and 5 years thereafter. CD screening should be considered at other times in patients with symptoms suggestive of CD. More research is required to determine the screening frequency beyond 5 years of diabetes duration.
passage_3: "Sex- and age-dependent effects of celiac disease on growth and weight gain in children with type 1 diabetes: analysis of the Type 1 Diabetes Exchange Clinic Registry" reports that celiac disease (CD) is common in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and effects of CD on growth in children with T1D remain unclear. We analyzed heights, weights, and body mass index (BMI) in 215 matched pediatric CD/control pairs in the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry. CD was defined by a clinic-reported diagnosis and positive celiac serology (n = 80) and/or positive small bowel biopsy (n = 135). Cases and controls were matched by age (mean: 14 years), diabetes duration (median: 7 years), sex (57% female), and clinic site. There were 5569 height/weight measurements. Gluten was restricted for varying periods of time in 61% of females and 51% of males with CD. Females with CD were shorter than female controls at all ages (P = 0.01). Weight z-scores were initially lower in preschool females with CD but similar to controls by middle childhood. Males with CD were initially shorter but adult heights were similar. Height in both sexes and weight in males were lower in CD participants diagnosed at younger age. Growth in T1D children with biopsy-proven CD, 76% of them were gluten-restricted, was comparable to that of T1D controls. We concluded that concurrent CD impairs linear growth in T1D females at all stages of development and in young T1D males. Young females with CD have lower weights, but both sexes have similar weights by middle childhood. Children younger at CD onset remain shorter throughout childhood; males younger at CD onset have persistently lower weights. Long-term gluten restriction may restore weight gain and linear growth in children with CD and T1D.

question: What were the main findings of the Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use.txt study?
passage_1: The study Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use evaluates whether youth involvement in the decision to initiate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) influences subsequent CGM adherence, and tests whether CGM self-efficacy and perceived hassle mediate this relationship among parent-youth dyads. The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.
passage_2: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_3: "Use of Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes" evaluates the emerging roles, applications, and current research landscape of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) technology in youth-onset type 2 diabetes. The review finds that CGM provides critical insights into free-living glycemic patterns, glucose variability, and cardiometabolic risk markers in obese and at-risk youth, revealing key discrepancies when compared to traditional screening tests like HbA1c and oral glucose tolerance tests. However, it highlights that interventional evidence regarding CGM's effectiveness in directly improving long-term glycemic control specifically in youth with type 2 diabetes remains very limited. Consequently, the paper recommends conducting rigorous future studies to address these knowledge gaps and establish dedicated guidelines for utilizing advanced glucose monitoring tools to optimize clinical outcomes in this young population facing an aggressive form of the disease.
